a wheel says what it does, and does what it says. Filed catalog because the item settled is the one this axis has named its largest since R1554 -- `External::wheel` had exactly TWO widget implementors, so a combo box and a tab bar answered no wheel -- and BOTH halves are now measured against the floor rather than assumed: the tab bar's is real and is BUILT, the combo box's is a HAZARD and is refused on purpose. The axis COMPLETION HOLDS AT 99 and the re-judgment says why: the remaining point was never the wheel alone, and what is left is three absent widget kinds (dial, font picker, a canned message box). *****THE ROUND BUILT THE LIST HALF WRONG AND THE TREE CAUGHT IT. A list was given a wheel that walked its cursor, on the reasoning that a combo box does that on the floor, and `hello-listbox`'s own wheel demo went red because a scrolling list stopped scrolling. Measured instead of argued -- 40 rows, current row 5, one notch -- the floor answers `currentRow 5 -> 5, scrollbar 0 -> 3`: a list SCROLLS and leaves the choice alone, which this tree already did for free because declining hands the event to the scroll chain. What steps on the floor is the CLOSED, UNFOCUSED combo box's value (index 1 -> 2), and that is the thing refused here on purpose. So the count is THREE implementors, not four, and the demo's combo-box check asserts what does NOT move. *****THE SCREEN ADVERTISED A GESTURE IT DID NOT HAVE, FOR ITS WHOLE LIFE. The analysis tool's node canvas prints `wheel = zoom` on its hint strip where a person reads it; a person reported that it does not, and measured again at the start of this round, eight wheel events and two Ctrl-wheel events over the canvas left zoom at 84 and pan at 0,0. Every gate was green, and the reason is structural rather than sloppy: the operation table's `zoom` row is satisfied by the zoom BUTTONS, which work, so a join over OPERATIONS is blind to a claim about a GESTURE. The strip is a different population and now has its own gate, over its own list, driven through the screen's real pointer and wheel entry points -- and it drives all four claims, not the one that was broken. *****A WHEEL IS THE ONE POINTER GESTURE WHOSE MEANING IS PURE LOCAL POLICY, and nothing anywhere could ask what it is. Measured on the reference toolkit at 6.11.1 by building a probe and running it offscreen rather than by reading documentation: across the four widget classes that answer a wheel there, 309 introspectable properties and 172 introspectable methods name the wheel ZERO times. The same probe measured what the silence costs -- a CLOSED, UNFOCUSED combo box in a form steps its value on a wheel aimed at the form (index 1 -> 2 unfocused, 2 -> 3 focused) -- and there is no property on that widget that lets the form find out beforehand, ask it to stop, or learn afterwards which control ate the scroll. ****SO THE DECLARATION IS THE PRECONDITION OF DISPATCH, not a description beside it. `External::wheel_intent(at)` says what a wheel at a point does; the router offers `External::wheel` ONLY where that answers Some; `scene/wheel_intent` publishes the same value the router routed by, at the point asked, through the router's own resolution. A wrong answer is therefore not expressible: removing the declaration removes the behaviour. A closed combo box declares nothing and the form keeps its scroll; a tab STRIP declares itself one and walks; a form's radio set declares nothing, and one type serves both roles so the role is declared rather than guessed. *****THE ROUND'S OWN MEASUREMENT CAUGHT THE DRIFT IT EXISTS TO PREVENT, one minute after the first wheel worked. The first draft asked the surface with no point, and since a screen is ONE External (2 #7) the wire then said "a wheel here zooms" over the palette, where the handler declines and the pane scrolls. The published answer was coarser than the behaviour it claimed to be; the fix was a parameter on the trait method, not care at the call site. ****THE PHASE WINIT REPORTS WAS BEING DISCARDED AT THE BOUNDARY (`MouseWheel { delta, .. }`) for the whole life of this shell, so the one rule it exists for had nowhere to live: a stepped widget drops its banked sub-notch remainder when the gesture ENDS, or a trackpad flick leaves a fraction of a notch for the next gesture -- minutes later, aimed at something else -- to spend. Reused GesturePhase rather than adding a wheel-shaped copy of its four arms. ****THE ARITHMETIC IS THE BEHAVIOUR CANON'S AND THE SUBSTRATE'S: one event is one step whichever way the platform sizes a notch (the direction is read, the magnitude is not), the step is multiplicative so out and back is the identity, and the anchor is Camera::zoomed_at -- the seats zoom about the middle and the wheel about the cursor, which are the same operation with a different point. `point_canvas_at` had the middle baked in twice and would have silently turned a cursor-anchored zoom into a centred one. Measured on the paint: five steps out and five back land exactly where they started, and the point under the cursor holds within a pixel across four steps. ****SIXTEEN COUNTERFACTUALS, and the one that PASSED was a finding: nothing in pinion-core asserted what UNIT a catalog widget declares, so a slider could claim to step ITEMS and every unit test agreed. Closed with a table over the six catalog wheels, four declaring and two declining, which is also what makes a fifth wheel added without a row visible.

an affordance leaves with the thing it is attached to. Filed dcc: this is the node canvas, and what it repairs is the picked link's floating column -- a node-graph gesture, not a catalogue widget. *****REPORTED BY A PERSON DRIVING THE RUNNING APPLICATION, one hour after a round that drove this screen through twenty demos with every gate green. Pan the canvas and the picked link's caption and its `delete` chip come along, pinned to the edge, while the link slides out of sight -- and measured, the second half is worse than the first: with neither endpoint painted, the chip held station at x=316 across pans of -949, -1898, -2847 and -3796, and PRESSING IT DELETED THE LINK, seven to six, with nothing on screen to say which one had gone. ****THE CLAMP IS RIGHT AND ITS DOMAIN WAS UNBOUNDED. R1681 added it because the card-avoidance search's first draft "pushed both endpoint seats out of the visible world entirely and traded one unreachable affordance for another" -- so it keeps a column being moved AROUND SOMETHING from being moved out of sight. It was never meant to fetch back a column the PAN carried away, and nothing said so. The behaviour canon settles the shape rather than leaving it a judgement call: it places the caption at the wire's own midpoint with no clamp at all and lets the viewport clip, so the bound is simply "if no part of the column is in view, do not move it" and R1653's clipping does the rest. ****WHY NO GATE SAW IT, which is the reusable half: every check panned ONCE. At a single pan the column tracks the graph to the pixel -- re-verified at four window sizes while diagnosing -- because the clamp only engages after the column's natural place has crossed the edge. A gate that drives a gesture a little cannot see a rule that only fires when it is driven a lot. *****TWO COUNTERFACTUALS, BOTH CAUGHT, AND THE SECOND PASSED TWICE FIRST -- each pass a finding. `all` in place of `any` switches the nudge off as soon as ONE part crosses the edge, the case R1681 built it for. It passed first because the assertion could not fail: "every part lies inside the canvas" is trivially true of a CLIPPED part, since clipping trims the reported rectangle to the edge -- the observable is the part's SIZE, 108x19 and 45x19 nudged versus narrower clipped. It passed again because the sweep's STRIDE was wrong for the geometry it samples: the two spellings differ only while the edge falls BETWEEN two parts, the parts are clustered (the chip sits inside the caption's 108 px span, 32 px in and 45 px wide), so the window is about 26 px and a 90 px stride steps over it. Eight pixels a step. ****AND THE AFTER-FIX MEASUREMENT WAS BRIEFLY WRONG IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: the first run still reported the ghost because it ran under PINION_ASSUME_BUILT against a binary the counterfactual driver had left behind. The tree's own recorded trap, walked into once more.

a canvas grid is declared, not enumerated. Filed perf because what moved is the cost model of a repeating fill and the axis's own name is pro-tool performance; the new `BoxStyle::lattice` is catalogue surface too, but the round's weight is that a picture which cost 95,131 painted nodes now costs one declaration. *****A PERSON REPORTED TWO THINGS AND THEY WERE ONE FACT: "the dots only go so far, so it doesn't feel infinite" and "zooming out is slow -- is this the floor's quality?". The answer to the second is NO, and the cause was the framework's rather than the screen's: pinion had no repeating fill, so a consumer wanting a canvas grid built it out of the only fill there was, a box per pip. Measured on the running application: zooming out took the painted scene from 12,879 nodes to 95,131 and a zoom step from 23 ms to 155 ms, every one of those nodes laid out, hit-tested, cached and published for a 1 px dot; and an enumerated lattice has to stop somewhere, so it was cut to a 6,400-unit world surface and panning past that edge left the canvas blank. ****THE FLOOR WAS MEASURED, not recalled -- a probe built at 6.11.1 and run offscreen over a scene one million units square. A tiled background brush costs 0.6-0.8 ms a frame and DOES NOT MOVE as the zoom falls; the hand-drawn variant stays under 2 ms while drawing 27,448 pips, because it paints into the exposed rectangle rather than materialising anything. Neither enumerates the scene, so neither can run out. AFTER: 12,879 -> 2,025 nodes, 95,131 -> 1,713, a zoom step flat at about 10 ms, and the grid full at pan -3,435. ****IT IS A DECLARATION, NOT A CALLBACK, which is what makes it legal under 2 #1 and better under 2 #7: a client used to receive 23,000 anonymous 1x1 boxes carrying no tag and no name, and now receives "a 1 px dot every 22 px, phased at (-60, -40)" and can place every dot from it. The wire got MORE knowable, not less. Where it goes was the real decision: on the world surface it would be bounded by the world exactly as the pips were, so it rides the VIEWPORT and the phase carries the pan -- which is what the behaviour canon does, parameterising a viewport background by zoom and pan. *****THE FIRST DRAFT DREW NOTHING AND EVERYTHING SAID IT WAS FINE. The scene was right, the declaration published, the node count fallen exactly as intended, every test green -- and the before and after screenshots looked the same BY EYE. A pixel scan said 1,731 grid-coloured pixels before and ZERO after: the world surface's opaque fill, invisible while it was the only ground, was a lid over every dot. The demo now asserts pixels, with the gap between two dots as a negative control. ****SIX COUNTERFACTUALS ALL CAUGHT, and CF-22 took three attempts of which all three faults were the counterfactual's rather than the gate's -- BROKEN by deleting the only call site (sixth instance of that class), then PASSED twice, once because the edit added the lattice instead of moving it and once because the find range left two `with_style` calls with the later winning. Reproducing by hand settled it. Writing CF-25 found a hole before it ran: nothing asserted that the phase carries the pan. ****FIVE GATES FIRED ON THE NEW FACET, each naming its repair: the facets destructure, the wire projection, the three-renderer parity matrix, and TWO demos whose census lists are hand-written on purpose -- their own message says the repair is to edit them, not to derive them, because deriving is how the wire and the type drift together in silence. And the counterfactual driver refused its first run on a red baseline, which is R1619's protection working. ****THIS ROUND ALSO REPAIRED THIS FILE: R1704's row had been inserted into the MIDDLE of R1703's, splitting it, and R1705's insertion split the result again. Restored from the last good revision and re-appended at the true row ends.

a selection is a set, and one of it leads. Filed dcc: multi-selection with an ACTIVE member is a node-editor capability, and this round is the node canvas -- the reference tool's frame gesture selects a host's cards and then carries them, and this screen had only the carrying. *****THE CAUSE WAS A TYPE, NOT A MISSING LINE: `Option<NodeId>` is a leader with no set, so "select these six" had nowhere to land. Measured on the running binary before the round -- pressing either host's tab left `selected` unchanged while six cards moved under the cursor. ****THE FLOOR WAS MEASURED BY BUILDING A PROBE AT 6.11.1 AND RUNNING IT OFFSCREEN, and it is short of this in both of its selection families: the free-form canvas one (the shape a node canvas IS) publishes 11 properties and 21 methods of which exactly TWO name selection and ZERO name a current, a primary, a lead or an anchor, its changed signal carries no arguments at all, and selecting three items leaves its focus item null; the item-model one does carry a current index and speaks only model indices, so it cannot address an item on a canvas. One member across all three of its selection-bearing classes names a reason, and that one is about focus. ***THE SAME HOLE IS IN THIS TREE TWICE and the other copy is the mirror image -- the material node editor holds a set with no leader, so selecting two of its nodes makes `query selected` answer NOTHING and its details panel, rename and dissolve all go dead. Registered rather than folded in: giving it a leader changes four behaviours it documents as deliberate, so it needs its own baseline. **`pinion_core::selection::Selection<T>` holds the members in arrival order and the leader AS AN INDEX INTO THEM, which makes "the inspector follows something that is not selected" unrepresentable; every mutation returns a Change naming what came, what went and where the leader was before and after. The free-floating cursor a keyboard walks without selecting is a different fact and already has a home in `widgets::roving`. *ALSO ON THIS AXIS: three outline states where there were two, `aria-selected` on the members with `aria-current` on the leader, a selection-count chip in the canon's own place, and `move_frame` -- so operation ten stops being one a person can cause and an agent cannot. **THE FRAMEWORK CORRECTED THE DRAFT: the leader was first spelled with `with_focused` and the a11y assembler cleared it on every card, because R1518 derives that flag from the focus the shell actually granted. It was right to; focus is where the keyboard is and the leader of a selection is `aria-current`.

a filter says what it keeps, and why it dropped the rest. Filed modelview: predicate filtering over a list is this axis's own slice -- its judgment names the floor's sort-filter proxy model explicitly -- and what moved is the vocabulary (two operators), the addressing (names, not ordinals) and the answer shape (a reason, not a boolean). *****THE SCREEN PAINTED A FILTER AND DID NOT FILTER. Measured on the built binary before the round, through the wire: the capture viewer's bar drew a three-clause query, three saved-filter chips and a 12,418 / 184,392 matched count, and the message list held its sixteen rows whatever any of them said. No `filter` verb (UnknownInvokePath), no text entry anywhere on the screen, and pressing a saved chip flipped a boolean, announced "applied units only", and moved nothing. Every check in that example was green throughout, because nothing had ever asked what the filter DID -- the same structural blind spot the sibling screen's operation table exists to remove. ****THE FLOOR WAS MEASURED BY BUILDING A PROBE AT 6.11.1 AND RUNNING IT OFFSCREEN, and it is short in five places at once: its row-filtering proxy filters on ONE column at a time (filterKeyColumn is a single int -- filtering column 1 gave 3 rows, then column 2 gave 2, where a conjunction gives 1, so the second predicate REPLACED the first), addresses that column by ORDINAL with no name-taking peer, offers three operator setters with no set membership and no inequality among them, publishes 12 properties and 101 methods of which six and eight name a filter and NOT ONE names a reason, and LOSES THE QUERY THE PERSON TYPED -- a wildcard set as `sensors/unit/*` reads back as the compiled `(?s:sensors/unit/[^/]*)`. ***THE ANSWER IS A LAYER, NOT A SCREEN FIX. `GridFilter` was already the predicate and is the wrong shape to type, to show or to save; `row_query::RowQuery` is the query as a person WRITES it, parsed against a roster of column names, keeping each clause's own source text, compiling to the `GridFilter` that does the work, with the facet index equal to the clause index so attribution reads straight through. `FilterOp` gains `Glob` (segment-aware, so `sensors/*/temp` rejects `sensors/a/b/temp` -- which `Contains` cannot) and `In`; `GridFilter::admit` names the FIRST facet that refused and `matches` is defined in terms of it so the two cannot drift. **TWO JUDGMENTS THE SCREEN FORCED. It opens UNFILTERED although the mockup shows a query in its bar, because that example's own row table states why it holds the rows it does -- a fragment run, a dropped piece, a declaration, an out-of-band payload, an unknown extension -- and a screen opening with thirteen of them hidden could not show what it exists to show; the reference query is preserved verbatim as the first saved filter instead. And the query text is the text FIELD'S OWN BUFFER rather than a Signal beside it, so the list filters live as the reference does and what the bar shows and what the list runs are one read. *THE FRAMEWORK CORRECTED THE DRAFT AGAIN: the buffer hook was first called inside the state factory and every test in the example failed identically on `Owner::cache` refusing to re-enter -- the documented rule doing its job rather than handing back a second buffer for the same tag. **ALSO: `Rect::contains_point` lifted out of the node lab, which was about to be copied here for the same click-to-caret reason; and this screen gets its first `spec::GESTURES`, so the gesture gate built one round ago now has a non-empty population on two screens of three.

a drag is answered once, and the frame says what it stood in for. Filed perf because what moved is the cost model of an interactive window resize and the axis's own name is pro-tool performance; the new `pinion_core::resize_batch` is substrate rather than catalogue surface, and the round's weight is that a gesture which cost 81 blocking paints now costs one. *****A PERSON REPORTED IT WHILE USING THE TOOL: grab a window edge, drag, and the INSIDE of the window falls behind the frame. Measured on a real mapped window driven by real window-system resizes -- not the RPC path, which mixes in a signal write -- and counted with the shell's own frame counter: 16 events / 16 frames / 340 ms to catch up after the last one; 40 / 41 / 1,119 ms; 80 / 81 / 2,693 ms. Eighty is about one second of a real drag. Nothing was slow: a resize frame measured CHEAPER than an idle one (11.6 ms against 20.2 ms). There were simply eighty of them and seventy-nine were superseded microseconds after they began. ****THE PRE-WORK MEASUREMENT CORRECTED THE DEBT FILE IT WAS PAYING. That file recorded "exactly two frames per resize event" and named settling why as the next round's first job. Re-measured: two per event is the RPC path's property (a signal write plus the OS echo), and the real winit path is one per event plus a constant. So the answer to the question was that its premise does not hold on the path a person drags, and the whole gap was that NOTHING COALESCED. ****THE FLOOR WAS BUILT, NOT READ -- a probe compiled against 6.11.1 and run offscreen, with forty resizes queued before the loop drains them. At its WINDOW layer it delivers all forty, in order, every intermediate size observable through an event filter. At its WIDGET layer it delivers ONE, carrying the final size, and paints once, in 4.4 ms. So the floor does not throttle the facts, it folds the work -- the right split, and this round adopts it. What the floor does not do is SAY that it folded: learning that thirty-nine sizes went unpainted means instrumenting both layers yourself and subtracting one count from the other, because no value there holds it. A first probe that only counted the widget layer had me believing it folded at the window layer too; the second probe overturned that, which is the round's reminder that a floor measurement also gets re-measured. ****WHAT SHIPPED IS A LAYER, NOT A SCREEN REPAIR. `pinion_core::resize_batch` holds one window's pending resize and the accounting of what folding cost. `note` receives EVERY event -- nothing is dropped at the report, only at the paint -- and answers `Noted::Opened` / `Superseded{size}` / `Repeated`, so a drop names its reason: a size that REPLACED pending work is not the same fact as one that repeated the size already pending, and collapsing them would make an idle window re-announcing its size read as a drag. `Fold::opened_at` remembers where the batch began, so the single frame answering a whole drag can state the span it covers rather than only its endpoint. `ResizeTally::is_balanced` is `events == painted + superseded + repeated + pending`, and it is PUBLISHED as `balanced` on `scene/frame_timings`.`resize` rather than left for a reader to re-derive. The shell's `note_window_resized` now only records; `about_to_wait` -- which winit reaches once the pending batch is exhausted and BEFORE the loop blocks -- drains and paints, so R1219's guarantee that a newly-exposed region is filled before the compositor composites is kept, per batch instead of per event. Measured after: 80 events, 2 frames, ~52 ms. ****AND THE RESIDUE WAS ISOLATED RATHER THAN GUESSED. With the paint folded, 80 events still held the event loop for 867 ms while drawing 2 frames (~33 ms of paint). Moving the surface reconfigure and the maximized query to the drain took that to 2.9 ms; putting the maximized query back per-event ALONE measured 3.9 ms, so the entire 867 ms was the wgpu surface reconfigure and the X round trip was innocent. The maximized query moved anyway, because the answer for a size a person is dragging through is not a state anything renders. ****A COUNTERFACTUAL PASSED AND REDESIGNED THE TYPE. Deleting the shell's paint call -- take the fold, draw nothing -- was caught by nothing: not the core tests, not the wire, not a three-screen integration test driving real windows. The cause was that the first draft counted the frame inside `take`, which is exactly what makes such a caller's books add up, and its own doc comment claimed the balance identity would catch it. The count now happens after the paint, via `painted(fold)`, and the interval between the two calls is deliberately unbalanced -- the only place that lie is visible. The same lie in a second spelling was closed with it: a zero-dimension fold is a minimize, `render_window` early-returns on one, so the drain now declines to take it and leaves it pending. ****THE INTEGRATION TEST DRIVES MAPPED WINDOWS, AND THAT IS A FINDING TOO. Resizing an UNMAPPED window leaves the GPU surface configured for a size the X drawable never took, and every subsequent swapchain acquire returns Outdated for ever: one resize takes `present_ok` from true to false, three ordinary ticks afterwards are false, and `scene/screenshot` answers RenderBackendUnavailable on every attempt including the third. Confirmed pre-existing against the stashed binary, and confirmed absent on a mapped window on the same host. Nothing had seen it because of a census that took a minute to run: of the demos in this tree that take a screenshot, ZERO also resize -- and `scene/snapshot from: paint` reads the ENCODED scene, which is built before the acquire, so every introspection surface reports a healthy window while nothing reaches the screen. This tree had never checked what is on screen after a resize; `r1708_a_drag_is_answered_once.py` is the first thing that does, on all three analyser screens, scanning the band of columns that only the widened window has.

a resize is followed by pixels, and a window that is dark says why. Declared `none` on R1606 / R1613 / R1650 / R1653's precedent: this round builds an instrument and pays a defect with it, and a swapchain recovery ladder is substrate under all eight axes rather than any one of them -- crediting perf would inflate an axis for work it is not named for (R1542's rule). *****R1708 FOUND, WHILE DOING SOMETHING ELSE, THAT ONE RESIZE OF A NEVER-MAPPED WINDOW LEFT IT UNABLE TO PRESENT FOR EVER: present_ok went true -> false and scene/screenshot answered RenderBackendUnavailable on every attempt afterwards, eight dead frames across two resizes, and a second resize did not recover it. Nothing had noticed because of the shape rather than the care: of the sixteen demos that take screenshots NONE also resized, and scene/snapshot from=paint reads the ENCODED scene, which is built before the swapchain is ever asked for an image -- so every introspection surface answers healthy about a window nobody can see. *****THE DEBT FILE'S OWN HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG AND SO WAS HALF ITS HEADLINE, which is the round's first finding. It said the surface was configured for a size the X drawable never took; measured, all three parties agreed -- xwininfo said 1100x700, winit inner_size() said 1100x700, the swapchain config was 1100x700 -- and it was still dead. Isolated in a 200-line reproducer with no framework in it: a frame after the window resized WITHOUT touching the surface presents fine; configure() to the new size makes every acquire outdated for ever; dropping the surface and making another one for the same window presents again. So the reconfigure is what poisons that swapchain, and it is exactly what this tree ran, once per failed frame, for ever, under a comment asserting it 're-establishes the swapchain so the NEXT frame acquires a fresh texture'. NOTHING HAD EVER CHECKED WHETHER THE NEXT FRAME DID. And the 2x2 says 'unmapped' names one cell of four: real Xorg x hidden is dead, real Xorg x mapped is fine, bare Xvfb is fine either way, same adapter -- R1708 had changed two variables at once and named the wrong one. *****WHAT REPLACES IT IS A LADDER, NOT A WORKAROUND. pinion_gpu::{Missed, Rung, SurfaceHealth}: the rung is chosen by how many attempts IN A ROW have failed since the last frame reached the screen, which makes 'did the previous response work?' structural -- if a rung worked the next frame presents, the count resets, and the ladder is never climbed. Reconfigure, then rebuild the surface, then repeat the cheap rung while saying everything known has been tried; Repeated deliberately does not give up, because a surface only reachable through a reconfigure would be dead for ever if it did. TWO COUNTERS BECAUSE THEY ANSWER DIFFERENT QUESTIONS: a frame missed because the surface BROKE and a frame missed because the window is merely WAITING (occluded, timed out) are both frames a viewer did not see, but only the first is evidence recovery is needed -- collapsing them would send a window that sat occluded five frames straight past the cheap rung to the exhausted one having tried nothing. *****THE FLOOR, BUILT AND RUN RATHER THAN READ: the reference toolkit's rendering-hardware-interface names four outcomes for a frame that missed the screen and publishes a per-window presentable fact, and gives the consumer NOTHING to remember it with -- no consecutive-failure count, no frames-since-last-present, no record that a recovery was attempted or whether it worked, no distinction between resize-the-swapchain and the-surface-must-be-remade, no reason for the last failure. Each proven ABSENT BY COMPILE FAILURE, five for five, which is a test rather than a reading. scene/render_fidelity now publishes all five, so an agent tells a one-frame blip from a window dark since the resize forty frames ago. *****TWO GAPS THE FIRST FIX LEFT, both found by re-measuring rather than by reasoning: scene/screenshot still errored for the frame right after a resize, so the capture path now CLIMBS the ladder inside the request while render still skips (a render loop is its own retry; a capture is an agent asking for a picture now, and there is no next frame unless someone asks), and a frame that missed the screen now ASKS for another one while a rung remains untried -- without it, since R1708 a resize batch paints exactly once, so a drag whose single answering frame failed leaves the window at the old size until an unrelated event repaints it. Measured after: screenshot never fails, at any size, on any of the three analyser screens. *****VERIFIED: 144 assertions over three screens in HIDDEN mode -- the one configuration every demo and all of CI runs in, and the one cell of the four where the defect occurs -- green on both the failing host (rebuilds 1, 2, 3, the driver defect made visible on the wire) and the bare offscreen server (rebuilds 0, the ladder correctly never needed), with identical ink counts. 12/12 counterfactuals, 8 unit and 4 integration. Blast radius 34/34: every demo in the tree that resizes or reads pixels. The E section of the demo would have been VACUOUS on a healthy host -- no reason is published when nothing breaks -- so the vocabulary assertion moved to Rust where it can always fail, and the demo now prints how many observations it actually got.

a resize says what it granted, and which declared bound moved it. Filed api: what moved is a routed method's published CONTRACT -- its response type, the vocabulary that response answers in, and a new dry-run mode -- which is this axis's own slice, and the wire census grew a type whose string vocabulary is sourced from the enum that owns it. *****THE WIRE ANSWERED WITH A NUMBER THE WINDOW DID NOT HAVE. Measured before the round on both displays this host has, driving the dashboard (which declares a floor of 1440x900) with a 1560x880 ask: on the bare offscreen server all of CI runs on the window really became 880 tall, because the declared floor was enforced by NOTHING; on the real desktop the window manager enforced it, the window sat at 900, and `scene/resize` answered `height: 880` on BOTH. Two defects hiding each other -- one no test could ever fail, and one that makes the §2 #2 path an agent drives report a size that does not exist. The `requested` field it answered beside it was a constant `true`: the `false` its own doc described was unreachable, because a missing closure returns Err. ****THE FLOOR WAS MEASURED BY BUILDING A PROBE AT 6.11.1 AND RUNNING IT OFFSCREEN, and it splits at exactly the layer that matters: its WIDGET layer resolves an ask against the declared bounds client-side (880 -> 900, 1340 -> 1440, the same on any display) while its WINDOW layer declares a minimum and then does not enforce it -- which is where this tree was, since a pinion shell window IS the window layer. That half is parity and this round takes it. Five things it lacks were each proven absent BY A COMPILE ERROR NAMING THE MEMBER rather than by a search that found nothing: a return value from resize(), a reason for a refusal, a per-axis which-bound-moved-me, a signal carrying asked and granted, and any way to ask WITHOUT acting; its window class publishes 18 properties and 52 methods of which zero name a reason and zero name a grant. ***THE ANSWER IS A VALUE TYPE, NOT A PATCH. `pinion_core::size_grant` holds the declared bounds, the per-axis verdict, and the resolution of one ask -- and `Grant` does NOT store the granted size, it derives it from the verdict, so a grant naming a floor cannot also report the asked number (the shape R1706's Selection took when it made its active member an index). `SizeBounds::new` refuses a floor above its ceiling, which is what leaves resolve with no precedence rule for a reader to learn. `applied` replaces `requested` and means dry-run and only dry-run, because an unreachable closure stays an Err -- one value must not answer two reasons (R1707). **THREE COUNTERFACTUALS PASSED AND BOTH FINDINGS WERE THE SAME SHAPE: A GATE DRIVING THE WRONG LAYER. The new demo measures each screen's floor instead of writing it down, which is right (one of the three screens declares a floor its design size is taller than) and which also made it blind to the shell stamping the WRONG floor -- every later section was self-consistent with whatever it was told. Fixed by reading the SECOND channel: the minimum the shell declared to the window system, back out of WM_NORMAL_HINTS through a libX11 probe, which works even for the unmapped windows the harness runs by default. And the only gate above `content_bounds` was the one binding that declares a ceiling, whose content bbox reaches NEITHER bound -- quadrupling the ceiling and dropping the floor to 1x1 both left it green -- so those moved to unit tests on the pure function. Final counterfactual tally 15/15. *ALSO: three hand-rolled clamp(min,max) sites lifted onto one home, a contradictory declaration no longer panics the render pass through u32::clamp, and `resize_and_settle` now waits for the size the response says was GRANTED, which is what makes R1708's demo pass under a window manager -- its real-path section ran on 3 of 3 screens where it had run on none.

a screen says how small it can get, and what stops it going smaller. Filed api on R1710's precedent: what moved is the published method surface -- a new routed read `scene/size_floor` with a censused response type, two declared vocabularies (verdict, refusal reason) and its own error, plus the FIRST parameter validation on `scene/scroll_reach` (`at`, refused by name as `InvalidAt`), which that method had silently ignored along with `viewport`, `width`/`height` and `dry_run` while answering about the live window every time. THE ROUND'S SUBJECT IS A NUMBER NOBODY CHECKED: 225 bindings declare a window floor and R1710 made the framework enforce it, but not one of those numbers had ever been driven against the screen it is about. R1710 tried, with the predicate a reader reaches for first -- is every declared region still painted -- and recorded five regions of the node lab as lost at its own floor. Re-measured here: all five are `scrollable`, each with the offset that shows it, and the screen's `lost` count there is zero. The diagnosis was wrong, the exemption table is deleted, and the gate now asks a question that needs no per-screen exemptions. THE OPPOSITE ERROR WAS ALSO MEASURED: at 1506 wide the node lab reports nothing out of sight because one pixel of a 100-pixel status chip is on screen and its 312-pixel inspector still starts at 1313 -- a floor derived from that is a floor at which the inspector is sliced. So `pinion_core::reach::cut` is a second derivation beside `out_of_sight`: what a size can never show WHOLE, judged against the viewport's reachable box rather than its shown one, which makes the answer independent of where the reader scrolled to. `pinion_core::size_floor` is the search: a bisection whose boundary is a pair it EVALUATED (the extent fits, one less does not) rather than one it inferred, refusing rather than answering when the ceiling itself does not fit or when nothing is ever lost, and `Measured::new` cannot build an answer whose evidence list is empty. THE PAIR IS A THIRD QUESTION AND IT ANSWERED NO: each axis is measured with the other at the ceiling, which is what a window minimum IS, and the pair of the two answers lost nine marks on the node lab and twelve on the capture viewer -- because `external::layout_size` fell back to the design size when EITHER axis was under its floor, so narrowing a window un-shortened its layout. That clamp is per-axis now, it has its first unit test in the round that found it, and the pair fits on all three screens. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT THEN FOUND: the capture viewer declared `SizeStrategy::Fixed` -- a window a reader cannot shrink at all -- while telling its own layout it lays out down to MIN_W x MIN_H, and those two numbers are exactly the measured floor (1425x346), 554 pixels shorter than the window would allow. It is `OpenResizable` now and the gate holds all three screens at verdict `exact`. BASELINE, measured at 6.11.1 with a probe built and run offscreen: the reference DOES derive a floor from its content and DOES enforce it client-side, and scrollable content correctly does not force it -- three parities, the third of which is this round's predicate. What it cannot do, each proven by a compile error naming the member (5/5): `minimumSizeHintReason` / `minimumSizeForcedBy` (the floor is a bare size and nothing says which child set it), `wouldFitAt` (no question about a size the window is not at), `unreachableAt` (no enumeration of what would be lost there) and `minimumSizeHintChanged` (no announcement, so a held floor cannot be known stale); 139 properties and 73 methods across its widget, layout and scroll-area classes carry ZERO reason names. *ALSO: R1710 left the wire-census integration test red -- it censused `SizeBound` for a type pinion-core owns, and the test demanded a local Serialize type of that name -- which the local gate could not see because it runs --lib. Paid here: a FOREIGN list names such shapes with their Rust path and a new test checks each against JSON a real value produces, which is a stronger check than the source parse the local types get, and `serde(default)` is now read as the other spelling of an absent key. Counterfactuals 14/14 after one PASSED and was a finding: with the ceiling taken from the DECLARED floor instead of the live window every section stayed green, so the demo now asserts the number the search was run against.

a window says what it gives up to get smaller. Filed api on R1710/R1711's precedent: what moved is the published method surface -- `scene/size_floor` grew a censused response object (`ConcessionReport`, eleven fields, its own declared vocabulary of four words) and its verdict vocabulary grew a fifth word, `conceded`. THE ROUND'S SUBJECT IS TWO FACTS SPELLED AS ONE NUMBER: a screen has a size below which its LAYOUT stops reflowing and a size below which its WINDOW refuses to shrink, and measured before this round all three analyzer screens passed one constant to both -- not tidiness, but the absence of any way to say anything else. R1689 had written the cost down 23 rounds earlier ("a 1600-wide display no longer holds this screen. That is a real loss") and nothing could act on it, because lowering the number would have moved the layout too. `pinion_core::shrink::ShrinkPolicy` holds both numbers plus the regions the band between them clips; a contradictory pair is refused by a const constructor, so a bad declaration FAILS TO COMPILE, and `shrink::audit` checks the declaration against what the screen actually does at that floor -- what is clipped and, the part a concession can never excuse, what is out of reach altogether. The reference floor was measured by building a probe at 6.11.1: it HAS the two numbers and enforces them (parity, and this tree had one), and it has nothing that says what the band costs, no way to ask about a size the window is not at, no announcement when the boundary is crossed, and 0 of 139 properties + 73 methods whose name carries the idea. The node lab now concedes 119 pixels of width (floor 1506 vs layout minimum 1625, giving up `lab.appbar` and `lab.inspector`), which puts a 1600-pixel display back in range; the other two screens declare `rigid`, which is a decision rather than the absence of one.

whether a reader can see a mark is a question about the whole clip chain. Filed api on R1710/R1711/R1712's precedent: what moved is the published method surface -- `scene/scroll_reach` grew a third count (`clipped`) and a third word in the vocabulary its `reach` field answers in, and every viewport row grew a censused `declared` box beside the aperture, so a caller reads what the chain took away instead of inferring it. The framework half is that reachability now COMPOSES: each clip level is offered only what the level above can ever bring into view, a level the chain leaves nothing of seals so a pane off the window is one report rather than one per row, and "is it on screen" is asked of the walk's own clip fold instead of a second copy of it. The screen half is the node lab's window floor, wrong twice for two different reasons -- 1506 from the blind predicate, 1595 from the tag-keyed paint scan built to work around it -- and now the boundary the integration test bisects for itself: 1601, with five row glyphs lost one pixel below. No axis in the tally counts a predicate becoming able to see what it was blind to, which is the shape the three rounds before this one filed the same way.

a window smaller than its layout PANS over it instead of cutting into it. Filed api on the R1710-R1713 precedent: what moved is the published method surface -- `scene/size_floor` grew a `recourse` word on its concession object and a SIXTH verdict, `panned` (the same arithmetic as `conceded` and a different fact: the reader gave up nothing), and `scene/scroll_reach` replaced the single `to_x`/`to_y` offset on every scrollable row with `moves`, an ORDERED LIST of every viewport that has to move and where to. That list is the round: a window that is a viewport onto its own layout makes every clip chain on the three analysis-tool screens two levels deep, so the single offset stopped being incomplete and started being wrong -- measured, five glyphs the node lab put outside the window answered `scrollable to (0, 0)`, an offset their pane was already at. Framework side, `pinion_core::shrink` gained `Recourse{Clip,Pan}` + `ShrinkPolicy::panning` (two further const-panic refusals) and `shrink::pan`, which the shell applies at the one place all three paint-scene producers start from, so a screen cannot declare a pan and ship a clip; `external::layout_point`/`into_layout` carry the pointer expression three screens had been writing by hand, and the node lab deleted its own copy of the basis. The node lab floor went 1601 -> 748 with nothing out of reach at any width, paying the 1600-pixel display R1689 wrote a loss against.

the focus a dispatch leaves behind is resolved to a FIXED POINT, on every path out of the seam. Declared `none` on R1676 / R1696's precedent: a consumer-forced defect repair (sprag PINION-PR89) that turned into the design underneath it, with no Phase B capability counted and no axis re-judged. THE REPORTED DEFECT IS A HALF-RIGHT INFERENCE. `pointer_button_for_window` offers every button edge to a raw multi-button sink first, and a consumed edge bumped the revision, requested a redraw and RETURNED -- skipping `handle_tail`, whose last line was the product's only call to `drain_focus_mailboxes`. A raw edge really has no `DispatchTail`, but `handle_tail` carries TWO responsibilities (drain the tail; resolve the frame's focus) and "there is no tail" retires only the first. So a `focus_request` written inside `External::raw_pointer_button` waited for whatever dispatch came next: focus one input late AND that input swallowed, which by eye is indistinguishable from nothing happening. Owning the raw stream is exactly what suppresses `click_to_focus`, so the mailbox is the only channel such a widget has left -- reported as a pane hosting a mouse-reporting child program that could not be given the keyboard by clicking it. THE ONE-LINE FIX WAS NOT THE DESIGN, AND STOPPING THERE WOULD HAVE LEFT THE SAME BUG ONE LAYER IN: user code runs INSIDE a resolution pass -- `on_focus_change` observers, and the R1020 retry's `V::view` -- and a single-pass resolution deferred whatever they asked for to the next dispatch, which is the reported defect exactly, inside the method built to abolish it. So the resolution settles: it repeats until both mailboxes are empty, bounded at 8 passes, reporting and CLEARING a frame that cannot converge (leaving the request would put it on the next unrelated input -- the same bug wearing a different hat). Three things follow. A CAPABILITY: "I was told I have focus; the real target is my child" -- the toolkit's focus proxy, the web's `delegatesFocus` -- now lands in the same frame instead of one input late. IDEMPOTENCE: the mailboxes are empty on return, so a second call is a no-op by construction. And therefore STRUCTURE: both seams resolve on EVERY path out instead of on the paths somebody remembered, so a future arm added to that `match` inherits it -- and "the six non-raw arms are unchanged" became true by construction rather than by judgement. R1456 is untouched: its case puts both requests in one pass, and a later pass exists only where user code reacted. THE COUNTERFACTUALS FOUND TWO GAPS AND BOTH WERE THE ROUND'S OWN, both the same class -- a negative or bounded claim is only a check when the observable exists. Deleting the raw arm's `return` (edge delivered raw AND the GUI arc run) left every suite green, because the fixture's widgets had no `introspect_mut` and the legacy send wire had nowhere to arrive; the sink carries that wire now. Raising the settle bound 8 -> 200 also left everything green, because a bound that only has to terminate is satisfied by any number; the fixture counts focus-gained calls and the gate reads that count against a literal, on both backends, so the number is a decision taken twice. The harness produced the same shape twice more: a fixture whose hand-written rects the layout pass overwrote gave an EMPTY edge log under red focus assertions, and the self-check press's own undrained request rode into the next dispatch and overrode it -- the reported bug in miniature, inside the gate built to catch it. Final counterfactual tally 11/11 after runs of 5/6 and 4/5.

a settings row says where its value came from, and a row nobody wrote is nobody's to write. Filed dcc because the node inspector is that axis's artifact and this is a capability it did not have: ConfigField gains a provenance axis (Source::Derived carries the SOURCE NAME, not a bool) and a destination axis (Goes::Aside carries a word for what the row is instead), the refusals belong to the value rather than to a screen's manners, the seat at a row's trailing edge offers take-over where it used to offer removal, and ConfigForm::author names what it displaced. Measured on the mature toolkit at 6.11.1 by BUILDING and RUNNING a probe: it can derive a value (20 -> 42 when the source moved), and it answers "is this derived" with a bool, drops a derivation silently when written over, lets a non-editable cell be written through the model, and has no reason channel at all -- 6 of 6 absences are compile errors there. Counterfactuals 23/23 caught over two plans.

a configuration row can have TWO contributors, and says which half is whose. Filed dcc for the same reason R1716 was: the node inspector is that axis's artifact and this is a capability it did not have. R1716's provenance had two answers -- somebody wrote it, or the screen worked it out -- and the behaviour canon's own screen needs three: a node may be told to dial an already-running peer this canvas does not draw AND be wired to the peers it does draw, which are two contributions to one list rather than two answers to one question. R1716 let the written value take the whole row and paid for the lost links with a gate warning; that payment is gone. ConfigField now holds the two halves (`written` + `worked_out`) and COMPUTES the shown value and the `Source`, so a form cannot be read back claiming to be authored while holding a derivation; `Source::Shared` is the third answer; `FieldType::merges` puts the composition rule on the SHAPE (a sequence composes, a single value contradicts) and `with_derived` refuses rather than picking a winner; `edited` moved to the written half, which was the question R1716 could not answer and its real reason for not composing. Provenance reaches the ELEMENT (`element_source`) because editing does -- driven, an edit over a contributed line wrote the canvas's whole contribution into somebody's half and moved its neighbours. Third seat (`Seat::GiveBack`): removing a shared row takes the written half out and LEAVES the row. Floor measured by building a probe and running it at 6.11.1: it DOES compose two contributors (a settings store falls back to a second store and taking the written half away brings the other back) so the capability is parity, and four absences are measured -- the composition is whole-key rather than element-wise (1 element answered where 4 were contributed), no reader can ask which store answered, a contribution ENDS a binding, and a cell holding a composed value answers 2 of 256 roles with none of them being how much of it is not yours. 6/6 absences proven as compile errors.

a type that speaks to a person says every sentence it can say, and a reader can tell them apart. Declared `none` deliberately: this round creates no widget and moves nothing a tally counting artifacts could see -- it is a gate over the wordings the tree already had, and the honest place for it is the ledger, not an axis. The defect it is earned by shipped in R1716 with every gate green: a fourth situation was added to a screen's launch panel with no wording of its own, fell through to another type's arm, and told a person the card's name twice followed by a sentence about unknown keys that was not about one. R1717 found it by photographing the panel. Measured before building: of the wordings this workspace can put in front of a person, 11 of 39 were read by any test or demo at all, and the unread include the launch verdict a screen paints into two toasts, the take-over toast, two of three configuration defects, and every reason a shut affordance gives a screen reader. `pinion_core::test_fixtures::speech` asserts four properties, each earned by a defect this tree had -- every arm is DRIVEN, silence is DECLARED both ways, all sentences are DISTINCT, and a clause OMITS the subject its caller prefixes. The silence split is the round's own correction, made by the first two types the gate was pointed at disagreeing about whether a good case speaks. The census reads the crate's own source twice (types that CAN speak, names actually driven) and asserts set equality in both directions, so there is no roster to keep in step; three crates call it and it refused four headers while being written, each refusal a real gap. Twice the round walked into its own class: the counterfactual driver refused a red baseline because the gate only existed when a sibling crate was in the same invocation, and three counterfactuals PASSED because the census's own failure branches were never driven -- both repaired, 8/8 caught after. Floor measured by building a probe and running it at 6.11.1: counting a speaking enum's arms is parity (4 of 4), and four absences are measured -- nothing reachable from the type enumerates the sentences it can say, the message census that exists is keyed by the SOURCE TEXT so two situations worded alike merge into one entry, it counts sources rather than sentences produced, and a refusal carries no sentence at all. 6/6 absences proven as compile errors.

what a screen says to a person is a VALUE that knows what kind of thing it is, and the kind decides how it is heard and how it is drawn. Declared `none` on R1718's precedent: this round creates no widget and no axis's census counts a capability it adds, because what it changes is a fact ABOUT the wordings the tree already had. Measured by driving the three screens: each kept "the last thing I said" as a String at 117 call sites (58/11/48), the wire typed all three `string`, and so the live region's urgency was a per-screen constant -- the node lab announced every confirmation `assertive` (a screen reader was interrupted for `selected R-01`) while the other two announced every refusal `polite`. An act that changed nothing said nothing at all and left the previous message standing. `pinion_core::utterance` gives the fact a type (a Tone plus the producer's own clause, stored unframed), `pinion_a11y::AccessLive::for_urgency` derives the urgency and the toast's bullet derives its colour, so neither can be set to a constant that is right for half of what a screen says. Floor measured by building a probe and running it against 6.11.1: its status channel carries no kind at all (0 of 62 properties + 37 methods), its dialogs have a kind of five arms that does not change the accessible role, its announcement event's politeness is a value the caller passes derived from nothing, and nothing refuses `refused: refused: refused: ` or the empty string. 6/6 absences proven as compile errors.

a refusal handed to the agent is heard by the person, and both channels branch from one value. Filed api on the R1710-R1714 precedent: what moved is the published refusal surface -- `error.data` grew an `announced` record naming whether the person was told and which live region carries it, on BOTH mutation channels, and every arm of the two refusal vocabularies (11 + 11) gained a person-facing sentence beside the tag an agent matches on. Measured before by driving every action slot the three analyzer screens DECLARE: 55 refuse and 2 reached the person, those two being the sites where somebody had written the coupling out by hand. After: 55 of 55, gated by a harness check that drives each surface's own declared action list rather than a sample, and asserts the named live region really carries the sentence. Reads are deliberately outside the seam. The round's own gate found two defects on its first run: a Rust `Debug` spelling reaching both channels on two screens (repaired with `IntrospectValue::kind`, R1699's defect alive on the agent's side), and one fact with two wordings on the node lab's link authoring. Floor measured by building a probe and running it against 6.11.1: refusing a call emits 0 accessibility events, the caller's whole answer is a boolean, the reason goes to a global diagnostic sink, its own status channel emits 0 accessibility events and takes no kind, and nothing anywhere reports whether the person was told. 6/6 absences proven as compile errors.

a row of chips declares how many of its members may be on, and its group role, its member role, the attribute carrying on-ness, its Tab-stop count, its arrows and its refusal are all derived from that one word. Filed catalog because the framework gained a WIDGET: `pinion_core::widgets::chip_group` (the rule, the roster, what choosing does, the utterance it says), `pinion_a11y::chip_group` (the only place the roles are spelled, dispatching to the three node families this crate already had), and `pinion_widget_paint::chip::chip_row` (the pill, carrying the focusability the rule derives rather than the parameter the module header had argued must stay a parameter). Four bindings adopted it and all three arms of the rule now have a live consumer: hello-packet-view and hello-analyzer-shell at-most-one, hello-filter-chip any, hello-segmented-button exactly-one. What earned it, measured 2026-08-19 by driving the running screens rather than reading them: the capture viewer BEHAVED as at-most-one (choosing a second chip cleared the first, choosing the chosen one cleared it) while announcing three independent toggle buttons over three Tab stops, and its own test file called them independent switches; the dashboard announced five operable toggle buttons whose pointer presses changed nothing and which no keyboard could reach at all. Two of three screens announced a rule they did not obey, and the third was right by memory rather than by construction. The floor was measured by building a probe against 6.11.1 and running it offscreen: the rule never reaches the accessibility tree (an exclusive set and an independent one report the same push-button member role), the object carrying the rule is not a widget so nothing stands for the set, at-most-one is not expressible at all, the group publishes a bare boolean beside its name, joining a group COSTS the keyboard (three loose checkable buttons are three Tab stops; the moment they join a group -- even a non-exclusive one -- two of them accept neither Tab nor an arrow and are reachable only by pointer), and Home/End move nothing inside the set.

a chart's legend is a declared chip row over its own named parts, and one word gives the row's shape, its accessibility node, its Tab stops, its keyboard, its on-state and its refusal. Filed dataviz because the charting axis gained a capability across its chart kinds: `pinion_chart::legend` (the declaration, the derived chip row, the only painter, the refusal that carries a sentence) plus `ChartLegend`, the trait EVERY chart kind implements so a board holding charts of several kinds can ASK before it offers the gesture. What earned it, measured 2026-08-19 against the compiled public surface rather than by reading paint: of seven chart kinds naming their parts, exactly two offered "hide this part by pressing its legend entry" and nothing anywhere said which two, so a board either knew by having read the crate or offered an affordance that did nothing. The two that did offer it each chose per paint, branching on an `Option<Vec<String>>` of caller tags that were zipped against the series, so a caller passing too few silently truncated its own legend; and the entries were derived six times over four files. After: polar and donut offer it for the first time, the three kinds that hold ONE set over a category axis answer with an empty roster (the truthful answer, and the one a board could not previously get), the tags are derived from each chart's own prefix, and the accessibility tree is R1721's chip-row derivation rather than anything new -- the legend is that widget's fourth consumer and its first inside a framework crate. The declaration is a precondition of dispatch: pressing a legend that declared itself paint is refused with the sentence a person is shown. Floor measured at 6.11.1 by reading both of its chart modules, since neither is built here and the module doc says so: it is AHEAD on breadth (six legend-marker kinds, one per series family, which is why this round's breadth exists) and a floor everywhere else -- a marker emits a click notification and nothing more so hiding the series is application work, a marker handles a hover event and no key event so the row is pointer-only, NEITHER MODULE CONTAINS A SINGLE ACCESSIBILITY CALL (measured across both trees, the count is zero), nothing declares whether a part may be hidden, and its successor module publishes `{colour, borderColour, label}` with no identity, no state and no signal. Obligation 3b caught a duplication the round had itself created -- six byte-identical `legend_seat` bodies, lifted into a trait default with the donut the only override. A counterfactual PASSED and the finding was the round's own test fixture: it hid the first part of two cards at once, which made a card reading its neighbour's toggle run produce the identical scene.

a drag stops asking the display server where every window is. (The axis key here is the TALLY's `perf`, which is a different vocabulary from COMMIT_FORMAT's type list -- that one has no `perf`, and this round's first commit message was rejected for using it.) Filed perf because what moved is the cost of a gesture, not a capability: dragging a window asked EVERY live window for its position on EVERY pointer event, and on X11 that question is XTranslateCoordinates -- a synchronous round trip -- plus a String allocation per window and a fresh Vec per event, so the cost was windows x pointer events blocking round trips and was linear in how many windows were open. A consumer dragging a terminal window between docks reported it, and the cause was found by following the call path rather than by profiling: the query sits three frames below the event, behind a gate whose own doc says it exists so that idle hovers and single-window apps skip it -- the author saw the cost and gated the case that was cheap to gate, leaving the expensive one running per event. `OriginFreshness` holds a generation and NO coordinates: the coordinates are the core's and are already there, and what was missing was the answer to "is what you hold still true", which is a question about events rather than geometry. Per-move round trips go from one-per-window to zero, and a move, a scale change or a change to the set of windows makes them stale again. The gate is a COUNT, not a clock: 240 pointer events collect once, because a wall-clock assertion over a display-server round trip is a flake generator and the count is what the defect actually was. ★ The round's own first cut reintroduced the whole defect and nothing caught it: the invalidation was placed before the tracked-window lookup, and the shell-private drag preview window -- moved by set_outer_position on every pointer event and deliberately kept out of the tracked set -- invalidated the cache once per event, during the very gesture the cache exists for. A counterfactual that restored that ordering was caught by NOTHING, because a unit test of the pure type cannot see a window that does not exist there. The repair was to move the tracked condition INSIDE the pure type, where flipping it breaks a test: an ordering is not a gate.

the analysis tool is one application at three of its seven seats, and a screen is a binding you can arrive at. Filed catalog for R1695's reason -- what this adds is the OTHER HALF of the paged region that axis opened: R1695 gave a destination a model and a rectangle, and this gives it a PAGE when the page is a whole binding with its own externals, its own keymap, its own accessibility tree and its own text caret. New crate `pinion-screen`: `Screen` (object-safe, NO default methods, so a hook added there stops `Mount` compiling until it is forwarded), `Mount<V>` (any existing `WidgetView` becomes a page, unedited), `ScreenRoster` (the only way to reach a screen, so "the screen you are not at is not routable, not keyable, not readable and not painted" is a property of the type rather than a rule an author keeps), and `coverage` -- a census that reads WidgetCore / WidgetA11y / WidgetView from their own SOURCE and fails unless each of their hooks is mirrored, folded into one of Screen's methods, or pinned as the host's WITH THE REASON. `hello-node-lab` (20,655 lines) is mounted at Catalog without one line of it changing: 139 tagged regions of it paint inside the shell, and the seat stopped saying `Unavailable::elsewhere` -- *built, shipping, and not here*. Two framework repairs were FORCED by the first real mount rather than reasoned into existence: `pinion_core::with_surface_extent` closes the limit R1700 wrote down and parked for want of a consumer (inside a view `layout_size` answered the WINDOW, and R1700 guessed the fix was reading the previous frame's rectangle -- it is not, because whoever placed the surface knows its extent before the view runs), and `CoreShell` now reads `V::read_state` inside the binding's owner scope, the wrap `V::view` / `V::apply_key` / `V::update` have had since R51.146 and which was missing two lines from its own `V::update` inside `route_intent_through_update`, unnoticed because none of this tree's 236 `read_state` implementations reads a hook. THE ROUND CORRECTED ITS OWN DESIGN FROM A MEASUREMENT: `shrink_policy` was pinned as window-level, and then the lab (layout minimum 1625 wide) placed in a 1388-wide region painted 51 of its regions outside that rectangle with its inspector running from x=1365 to x=1677 in a window that ends at 1440 -- the screen had declared `Recourse::Pan` since R1714 and the region was not listening. Four of the shell's own censuses assumed it owns every page and now say which destinations they are complete for; two tools keyed their population on `examples/*/src/main.rs` and would have gone quiet about a binding that became a library rather than reporting it missing.

what a surface is holding paints in front of what it is not, and being held is one declaration the paint order, the hit order and the elevation all come out of. Filed catalog because the framework gained an interaction capability every canvas and every board needs: `pinion_core::held` -- `Held` (a SET, because the second consumer drags a whole selection), `HELD_SHADOW`, `raise_to_front` (the derivation) and `ContainerNode::with_held` / `with_held_group` (the builder over it). One call REORDERS, RECORDS and RAISES. It reorders rather than setting a flag a later pass consults, and that is the design: the child order IS the z-order, since a scene paints depth-first and `Scene::hit_test` walks the same children in reverse -- so a flag would be a second source for that order and the two would disagree the first time anything else read `children`. `hit_test` needed no edit at all. What earned it, measured as paint order on BOTH of this tree's node graphs: the dragged item painted BEHIND the one it was over (hello-node-lab index 70 against 80, hello-node-editor 12 against 15), so the stationary card's opaque body covered it. The owner reported that as three separate complaints -- the card goes grey, they do not overlap, is not overlapping better -- and all three were that one fact: they DO overlap (after a drag the two sit two pixels apart), and overlap is not what was wrong. THE SECOND AND THIRD CONSUMERS EACH CORRECTED THE API BEFORE IT SHIPPED: the editor drags a selection rigidly, so a single-tag declaration would have been wrong on its SECOND use rather than its third; and the dashboard hands its cards straight to a pane helper and never holds a container, so the builder form could not reach it and the derivation became a function with the builder calling it -- one implementation, two entry points. A TRANSIENT LIFT IS ONLY HALF: released, the card returned to specification order and went straight back under what it had been dropped on, so each screen now owns a stacking order that a pick-up raises and a drop keeps; position is untouched, because on a free canvas a drop displaces nothing (the rule every node editor keeps, and the opposite of this tree's tile dashboard, which reflows and reports what it displaced). Floor measured by building a probe against 6.11.1 and running it: it HAS a per-item z and its paint and hit orders agree, but pressing or dragging a movable item does not raise it (the back item stayed behind through press, march and release), there is no notion of *held* at all (`isSelected` and `isUnderMouse` exist; neither means "is being dragged"), and elevation derives from nothing -- a mechanism and no rule, which is why applications there write the raise by hand. ★★★★★ THE ROUND'S LARGEST FINDING IS ABOUT ITS OWN VERIFICATION AND THE OWNER FOUND IT: asked why the drags were not being performed directly, and whether having to ask what the screen was doing was itself an architectural defect. Measured, the harness's `scene/drag` makes the dragged card follow the cursor while a real pointer leaves it in place, moves a snap mark and reflows on release -- so every green it gave was about a gesture nobody performs, and three further defects were hiding behind those greens: an opaque drop preview covering the widget under it (an opaque preview has NO correct layer -- under the cards it hides behind the destination, over them it hides what is standing there, and both reach a person as "the widget goes grey"), a cell computation that ignored the board's scroll while the hit test folded it (so a press after scrolling selected one card and dragged another), and the absent cursor label the behaviour reference carries. Two of this round's own tests were also wrong and each taught something: one scrolled a board whose scroll range was zero, so it measured nothing and would have passed for a function that ignores the offset, and one asserted the carried chip paints last in the WINDOW when the window's last thing is the palette.

a screen draws its own navigation only where it is the one providing it, and what a place already has is a fact the place STATES. Filed catalog because the framework gained a capability every composed application needs: `pinion_core::chrome` -- `Part` (the closed vocabulary: Navigation, ApplicationBar), `HostChrome` (a set, not a boolean, because a host with a rail and no bar is the ordinary arrangement and a guest deciding what to omit needs the difference), and `with_host_chrome` / `host_chrome`, a scope in exactly the shape R1724's `with_surface_extent` took. What earned it, measured on the running application rather than read: R1724's first mount put two navigations in one window -- the shell's rail at x=0..52 and the mounted screen's own at x=52..106 -- and the accessibility tree published BOTH as role=navigation, named Destinations and sections. Neither screen was wrong, which is why the repair is in neither: a screen that has ever run standalone needs a navigation, and that need stops being true the moment it is placed inside an application that has one, which is a fact about THE PLACE. THE AUDIT INVERTED THE PREMISE THE ROUND WAS OPENED WITH, and it cost thirty seconds: extracted from the behaviour reference's three screens, it draws ONE rail of EIGHT seats, identical on every screen with only the active marker differing -- and against that the shell's rail is 7 and has no `Logs` while the guest's 7 are the reference's list minus `Settings`, so THE GUEST'S RAIL WAS THE CLOSER OF THE TWO. "It is a duplicate, delete the guest's" is a shape that can move a reproduction backwards; what made the deletion safe is a different measurement, that every seat of the guest's rail answers "<name> is not this screen" and navigates nowhere. The host's missing seat is registered as its own debt because closing it needs a vocabulary decision rather than code -- `Seat` offers Page, Elsewhere and Reserved, and "in the reference's first phase and simply not built" is none of the three. The guest derives FIVE things from one predicate (the paint, the accessibility tree, the reserved width, every pane rectangle, and therefore what the pointer can reach) because two readers of one fact is what produces a screen that publishes a rule it does not keep; `RAIL_W` stays a constant because it is also a window-policy number and that ask does not change with where a page happens to be. Floor measured by building a probe against 6.11.1 and running it: a complete application window placed inside another application's page container keeps its menu bar (23 px), its tool bar and its status bar; its accessibility tree carries 2 MENU BARS, 2 TOOL BARS AND 2 STATUS BARS; and there is no property, method or event by which the guest could ask -- the nearest signal is window(), which answers the HOST's window, so a guest can learn THAT it is embedded and nothing about what that place has. A COUNTERFACTUAL PASSED AND IT WAS A DEFECT IN THIS ROUND'S OWN GATE: the shell's assertion was `rect_for_tag(..).is_none()`, which answers None both for a tag no node carries AND for a node whose rect does not resolve, so restoring the unconditional rail was invisible -- the width still derived from the same predicate and the node came out zero-wide, which is exactly the case the round's own documentation says must not pass. The assertion is now over `Scene::tags()`, presence rather than geometry, and the class was audited: the only two other absence-through-rect assertions in the tree are sound.

a captured pointer carries the rectangle it was measured over, so a gesture reads one fact instead of two at two different times. Filed dcc because the three consumers the census turned up are this axis's three widgets -- the node graph, the data grid's column resize and the tile board -- and each was scaling a painted fraction by something read from the live model. Measured on the dashboard, one press from the same pixel to the same pixel: a real X11 pointer and eight separate `scene/drag` calls both left `loss@0,4 latency@0,5 topology@0,6`, and ONE `scene/drag` with steps=8 left `loss@0,10 latency@0,7 topology@0,11`, because the harness's own march delivers the moves with no frame between them and a hand does not. `pinion_core::PointerReading` carries the fraction AND the extent of the rect it was taken over; `px()` is `cursor - rect.origin` whatever the model has done since. `External::pointer_move` takes it as one argument -- one spelling, so every implementor and call site had to say which unit it meant, which is what made the class visible. The migration touched 21 implementing files and 195 call sites; ask for today's population with `grep -rl 'fn pointer_move(&mut self' --include=*.rs crates/ examples/` rather than trusting this sentence, because the round that wrote it then ADDED implementors and calls of its own and the two numbers were stale within the hour. The column resize lost the `ScrollState` it carried solely to supply the second fact (the compiler's unused-import error is the proof). The node editor was multiplying a CANVAS fraction by the WHOLE surface -- `capture_normalize` names `Tag(GRAPH_TAG)`, `on_resize` fills `self.surface` with palette and detail panel included -- so its click-versus-drag dead zone was inflated by TOTAL_W/WIN_W, two rectangles in one function, and no test had ever stated which one it meant. Two gates land with it: `assert_gesture_reads_one_fact` (the same gesture as one call and as one call per move must leave the same state -- the class debt's own statement, no display needed) and `rpc_verify.RealPointer`, which moves the machine's own pointer, calibrates by asking the surface where it thinks the cursor is, and takes a `hold` callback that runs WITH THE BUTTON DOWN, so a demo reads the scene mid-gesture instead of asking a person. Floor, probed against 6.11.1: its move event carries widget-local pixels so the failure mode does not arise there -- on that axis the floor was above us -- but across six of its classes, 441 declared properties and 274 declared methods, not one names the extent a paint used and none names synthetic-versus-native.

an application's navigation can be checked against a navigation somebody wrote down, and a surface can say it is specified and not built yet. Filed catalog for R1695's and R1725's reason -- the rail and its roster are this axis's, and what this adds is the half that says whether the roster is the RIGHT one. Two framework additions. `UnavailableKind::Unbuilt` (7 arms -> 8) plus `Unavailable::unbuilt`: in the specification of the release being built, and not built. It earns an arm because all three neighbours say something false -- `Reserved` claims a later release when it is in this one, `Elsewhere` sends a reader to open a window nobody wrote, `Unsupported` says no action changes it when building it does -- and because without the sentence such a seat is either hidden (and the specification's shape is invisible) or it tells one of those three lies. Its `Recourse` is deliberately NOT a new arm: it shares `AwaitRelease` with `Reserved` because the reader's ACTION is the same and only the subject differs, which is the split `Unsupported | Unstated -> Nothing` already makes. And `RosterSpec` / `SeatSpec` / `Required` / `Divergence` in `widgets::destination`: a written-down navigation and a diff against a live `Destinations` that runs in BOTH directions at once -- absent seat, INVENTED seat, order, title, standing -- fixing the KIND of a closed seat's reason and leaving its wording to the application, so the check survives translation and still catches a seat closed for the wrong reason. THE SPECIFICATION IS A SEPARATE TRACKED ARTIFACT AND THAT IS THE DESIGN: `docs/analyzer-rail-spec.json` holds the reference's eight seats plus an `owed` list of accepted differences carrying the divergence VERBATIM, the round that accepted it and why; a specification written in the same file, in the same edit, by the same hand as the thing it judges is a gate asking its subject for the answer. The gate asserts EQUALITY with that list rather than containment, so paying a divergence off fails too and says "you fixed it, record it" -- the direction a floor cannot see. The application publishes the comparison on the wire (`conformance`: specified, reproduced, divergences, owed), because "open the log section" is a reasonable next move for an agent and the answer is *no, and here is why, and it is not the same why as the two seats waiting for a later release*. WHAT THE ROUND'S OPENING MEASUREMENT FOUND, and it was worse than the debt file it came from: the reference draws EIGHT seats in one order on all three of its screens and this application drew SEVEN -- three of whose keys the reference does not have, two of whose sections were missing from the rail entirely, and one of which (`decode`) was assumed to be half of the capture viewer when the reference's third section is a separate thing its behaviour prototype fully implements. THE NEW GATE THEN FOUND THREE MORE DEFECTS ON ITS FIRST THREE RUNS, all of which had survived every gate this screen had: a tag namespace where a seat and a non-seat chrome chip share the `shell.rail.` prefix (fixed by DERIVING the exclusion from the voice table rather than naming it, because an exception written as a list is only as good as whoever remembered to update it); the seat carrying the mounted node lab wearing the mark the reference gives its LOG section, with two further marks crossed the same way; and `sessions` and `settings` having no arm in the painter at all, falling through to its fallback, and being drawn IDENTICALLY -- two adjacent icons a reader cannot tell apart, on a screen whose whole subject is telling things apart. A seat and its icon had never been one fact and no test read both; the repair that does not require the reference's artwork in the repository is comparing the drawings WITH EACH OTHER. Floor: there is no row to compare on this axis, and that is the finding -- a paged container at 6.11 addresses pages by ordinal so reordering the rail and changing where a press goes are the same edit, carries one bool with no vocabulary for why a page is inert, arrives at a disabled page anyway, and leaves its accessible current-page value empty, so the statement this round checks cannot be written down there at all.
