Filed dcc because the widget it lands in is this axis's property grid (`pinion_widget_paint::config_form`, whose only consumer is the analysis tool's node lab) and because the control it replaces was that grid's, not a catalogue item added beside it. THE DEFECT, AS A NUMBER, BEFORE THE CHANGE: a `FieldType::Choice` row laid one chip per option from the control's left edge with no wrap, no clip and no scroll -- measured with the inspector's own `FormStyle::default()`, a three-word roster spends 229 px of a 284 px pane saying one word, a six-word roster runs 50 px PAST ITS OWN CONTROL and a seven-word one 113 px. The reference collapses the same field: its inspector derivation gives a field five mutually exclusive control kinds and draws the enumeration one as a closed control carrying the word it holds and an arrow, styled identically to the text field beside it. ONE FRAMEWORK ADDITION, `pinion_core::widgets::picker` -- `Picker` / `Picked` / `PickerDefect`: the TRANSIENT STATE OF CHOOSING, which is the roster and where in it the reader is, and deliberately NOT the value; the value stays in the document until a choice is committed. There is no `open` flag because a screen holding no picker has no open picker, so "shut and highlighting the fourth option" has no spelling. Its wire form goes back through the constructor's rule via `serde(try_from)`, because a snapshot is a door into the type as much as the constructor is and §2 #3's dry_run restores signals from one. THE FLOOR, PROBED BY BUILDING AGAINST 6.11.1 AND RUNNING IT with real key events under the offscreen platform, is where every member of this type comes from: NOTHING THERE ANSWERS WHAT COMMITTING RIGHT NOW WOULD CHOOSE -- of 123 members exactly two name the highlight and BOTH ARE SIGNALS, an event you had to be listening for; a check written the natural way PASSES while the reader is looking at another row (asserted the committed index while the open roster showed the fifth, and it held); an empty roster is accepted (count 0, index -1, empty text, no complaint); a word the roster does not offer is silently ignored, void return and no signal, and an index past the end is accepted and clears the control to nothing; a letter on the closed control COMMITS (the value moved from the first word to the fifth without the roster ever being shown) and typing it again over three words starting with it never leaves the second; arrows on the closed control commit one document write per press and do not wrap. Against each of those: `highlighted()` is a value, `over()` refuses an empty roster, `holding()` NAMES a word the roster lacks instead of substituting, `point_at()` refuses an index past the end, typeahead advances and wraps, and movement is not a write. THE PAINT SIDE: the roster is published as its own LAYER (`FormGeometry::popup`, `option_at`, `on_popup`) rather than as more of the open row's parts, because a hit test walking the rows in order would resolve a press on the roster to whichever row it covers -- the layering is a declared fact instead of a consequence of iteration order. The control's ARIA role moves from radiogroup to combobox with `expanded` derived from the geometry, so the announcement and the paint cannot disagree, and the arrow declares itself folded into the control rather than being announced as a second affordance. The type badge now carries HOW MANY WORDS ARE ON OFFER, which is the reference's own and which a collapsed control is exactly what makes necessary. THE INTEGRATION GATE IS THE OTHER HALF: `docs/analyzer-inspector-spec.json` is a separate tracked artifact holding three surfaces, and the screen's test reads each one BACK OUT OF THE PAINTED SCENE -- the row's parts in reading order, the roster's options titled by the RUN PAINTED INSIDE EACH ONE, and the five control kinds classified from the affordances actually drawn. Its ledger runs in BOTH directions: the two second-pass controls this build has and the reference does not (a clamping stepper for a bounded integer, per-element rows for an array) are RECORDED rather than deleted, which is the standing order rule made enforceable. Three findings the gates produced rather than reading did: the key run and the type badge had never carried tags at all, so the one thing on a row that says what it is about could not be addressed, read back or censused; tagging the key run tripped R1655's pointer-transparency gate on its first run; and the row's part tags come in TWO SHAPES -- `<family>.<key>` for most and `<family>.<key>.<discriminator>` for the ones a shape can have several of -- which made the first draft of the conformance reader report perm, int and list absent. a palette hands the board a footprint and the board says where it would land. Floor, measured by building two probes against 6.11.1 and running them: across its grid container, its layout base, its widget class and its item view NO member answers "where would a w-wide item land at this cell"; two items asked for the same cell both get geometry and OVERLAP with nothing to refuse with; a drag-move event carries a pixel and nothing turns it into the cell a release would use. Honest counter-measurement: on the neighbouring axis the floor is ABOVE us -- a target there accepts a payload from a source it has never heard of, negotiated by format, and pinion's drag session dispatches only to the source (registered, with the numbers, as debt-a-drop-target-never-sees-the-drag). Four findings the gates produced rather than reading did.

a drop target is asked before the drag, and can be asked before anything is picked up. Filed dcc because the gesture it completes is the IDE/DCC-class placement drag R1733 filed under the same axis -- a palette hands a board a footprint -- and because this axis's own widgets (property grid, node editor, tiling board) are where a cross-surface drop is a requirement rather than a hypothetical. THE HOLE: this framework's drag session spoke to exactly one party. `begin_drag` opened it and `drag_to` / `drag_release` / `drag_cancel` all went back to the surface that started it, which then decided on the destination's behalf what a release would mean. That works when one coordinator owns both ends, which every in-tree consumer happened to be, and a drop BETWEEN two surfaces could not be spelled at all -- R1733's palette-to-board satisfied the condition BY ACCIDENT, both halves living inside one composite External. THE FLOOR IS ABOVE US HERE and that is why the round exists; probes rebuilt against 6.11.1 and re-run at the start of this round rather than remembered: a target there receives enter 1 / move 3 / drop 1, each event carrying the payload's format list, the proposed action and the possible actions, and it accepted a payload in a format it had never heard of from a source that had never heard of it. AND THEN IT STOPS, in three measured places: you cannot ask before the drag (acceptance is one boolean per widget whose real decision lives inside an event handler that has to run; per-part acceptance is a second boolean and NAMES NO KIND -- three rows answered yes/no and not one could say what it would take; the members that do name kinds are plain virtuals absent from the runtime metaobject a generic reader walks); a refusal is a bare bool with no reason; and the preview and the commit are two computations, because the move event carries a PIXEL. THE BEHAVIOUR REFERENCE DOES EXACTLY THAT, measured in its own script rather than asserted about a toolkit: its palette tile sets effectAllowed='copy' on drag start, its board takes dragover / dragleave / drop, and its dragover computes the destination cell to draw the snap while its drop computes THE SAME CELL AGAIN to add the widget -- one fact, two computations, from two events; its board also raises the accept highlight for a kind it does not recognise, because acceptance is decided inside the handler that is already drawing. `pinion_core::drop_target` answers all four. A surface DECLARES what it takes as data (`DropContract` / `DropClause` / `DropRegion`, static and Copy like `IntrospectSchema` because the router asks on every cursor sample), published at the reserved `$drop` path beside `$schema`. a press lands where it was aimed, and the gate that watches it can see a rectangle instead of a point. Filed dcc because both halves land on the node editor -- this axis's node-graph third -- and because the defect was reported against it by a person using it. THE REPORT: "a node created from the palette cannot be selected", and decisively, "sometimes the node is selected and sometimes the background behind it is, so dragging pans". Every gate was green. FIRST FINDING, AND IT IS ABOUT MEASUREMENT ITSELF: the previous round's recorded reproduction was NOT a reproduction. Its probe pressed nine points inside a card with press-move-move-release, which is a DRAG, so each successful press carried the card away by the delta and the later points landed where the card no longer was; re-measured, the card's painted rect walks 428,143 -> 431,145 -> 434,147 across the probe, and feeding that drift back reproduces all nine rows of the table exactly. My own first re-run made the same 26-of-63 for the same reason. Drag-free, with a real X pointer and the rectangle re-read immediately before each aim: 63 of 63 at nine points per card, 56 of 56 at the exact edge and corner PIXELS, and the framework's census reports astray 0. A probe that disturbs what it measures measures the disturbance. SECOND FINDING, THE REAL ONE, ONE PIXEL: the router hands a screen a FRACTION of its surface and the screen multiplies it back, the fraction was made by an f32 division, and a truncating cast turns a product landing a hair below an integer into the pixel before it. Measured by walking a real pointer over 600 columns and 600 rows and asking the screen where it thought the pointer was: 35 of 600 columns and 20 of 600 rows arrived one pixel left or up, x=434 among them while 491 and 547 in the same sweep were exact. Counterfactual, cast reverted and rebuilt: the same 35 and 20; with the repair, 0 and 0. On a nine-pixel pin that is an eighth of the target, which is the shape of "it works and then it doesn't". `pinion_core::external::pixel_of` nudges the product by the largest error the f32 can carry -- derived from the format, not chosen -- and floors, so a genuinely fractional cursor still names the pixel it is inside; asserted over the WHOLE range of five extents rather than at a sample, because which pixels fail depends on the extent and any list somebody picks can miss them all. THIRD, THE GATE: `scene/pointer_target`'s eight non-centre probes only ever RESCUED a rectangle -- they ran when the centre disagreed and could turn Unreachable into Handle -- so in the direction that CONVICTS it sampled one point, and that point was the middle, which is the last point a transform error moves and the one every automatic observer in this tree aims at. All nine are asked now, always, and each answer is judged against the paint: an answer naming something else is sound exactly when the paint puts that something else at that very point, so a card's corner answering the pin that overhangs it is the paint agreeing with itself and the same corner answering the canvas behind it is the sixth verdict, `Astray`, which is a defect and which OUTRANKS a centre that agrees. FOURTH, AND THE PART NO FLOOR CAN REACH: `pinion_core::painted` keeps every tagged rectangle a surface's last frame drew, in paint order, in that surface's own coordinates, recorded on the same pass and from the same rectangles as the surface sizes. The node lab's canvas resolves its cards, its pins and the picked link's chrome from it, so the drawn rectangle and the pressed rectangle are ONE rectangle and the overlap priority is the paint's too -- the hand-written "chrome, then pins, then cards back to front" is gone, the pin is over the card because the painter drew it there, and the accept-pin's role check disappeared because the paint already encodes it. Stated rather than hidden and written into the spec file's owed ledger: a wire carries no tag so a press on one is still parsed from the model, and a host frame's grip is its strip which the paint does not name apart from the box. FLOOR, BUILT AND RUN AT 6.11.1: a canvas item that paints exactly the region it declares is pickable at 100% of the pixels it was drawn in under four camera transforms including fractional zooms (13,500 / 9,450 / 11,718 / 9,919 points, no misses) -- a real floor this tree owed. What it cannot do is notice the two coming apart: an item whose paint reaches six pixels past its pick shape leaves 15.4% of its painted pixels dead at zoom 100 and 84 and 30.1% at 135 while the framework holds BOTH rectangles, hands out the larger as the item's bounds and never compares them; and of eight marks a self-painting widget drew inside itself the framework names zero, because the only record it keeps of a paint is pixels. THE SELECTION SPEAKS on the pointer path now: the sentence sat in the wire's invoke arm rather than at the act, so the reader who uses the pointer heard nothing and the agent who uses the wire heard everything; it moved into `apply_selection`, the one place a selection changes, which also makes "a press that changes nothing says nothing" fall out of the early return it already had. THREE LIFTS from the third-consumer grep: `Rect::holds` for the integer-pixel predicate, `painted::probe_points` for the nine (the gate and the screen's own sweep must not hold two definitions of "the whole rectangle"), and `record_painted_surface` so the in-process sweep records what it painted exactly as the shell does -- without which the fixture would drive a hit test the running window does not have. `docs/analyzer-press-spec.json` is a separate tracked artifact with four surfaces, and `tools/demos/r1736_a_press_lands_where_it_was_aimed.py` reads every clause back with 13 named checks driven by the machine's own pointer, its own D-section marker deliberately another act's sentence so "said nothing" and "said the same thing again" are distinguishable. 5,759 tests across core, rpc and runtime; 97 node-lab tests; six blast-radius demos re-run green including the three the wire census named most-affected.

a pointer arrives where the pointer is: the framework records the arrival, compares its own two accounts of it, and publishes the verdict. Declared `none` on the R1650 / R1653 / R1676 / R1709 precedent -- this round builds an instrument and pays a measurement debt with it, and a new introspection READ is not what the api axis is judged on (that axis is stabilisation: schemas, versioning, deprecation, none of which moved). No widget, no gesture, no axis re-judged against measured evidence. WHAT THE ROUND FOUND AT ITS START, and it changed the debt's prescription rather than confirming it: R1736's repair of a one-pixel round trip was measured by walking a real X pointer over 600 columns and 600 rows of a running screen and asking the screen where it thought the pointer was -- and that only works on a screen which publishes a cursor. Measured across the five screens here that implement a hit test of their own: THREE publish one, in TWO incompatible spellings (an "x,y" string and an {x, y} object), and TWO publish nothing at all. So the check that found the defect was not runnable on two of the five, and on the other three it went through each screen's own vocabulary. The fact was never the screen's to volunteer. THE ROUTER HOLDS BOTH ACCOUNTS AND WAS DROPPING ONE: `capture_rel_coords` resolves the cursor against the rectangle the paint laid out and then discarded the ORIGIN, exactly as R1727 found it discarding the EXTENT. With both kept, the pixel the pointer is over is floor(cursor) - rect.origin -- arithmetic with no fraction in it -- while the pixel the surface will resolve is pixel_of(fraction, extent), and `pinion_core::arrival::Landing` is the framework comparing them. Three arms, no catch-all: Exact, Drifted{by} carrying which way the press moved, and Strayed, because a capture lock keeps forwarding after the cursor leaves the rectangle and the resolved pixel there is a clamp rather than a claim -- folding that into either neighbour would manufacture a defect out of correct behaviour. Recorded at the DELIVERY and only on the position channel: the wheel and two-finger channels read the fraction, so a pixel verdict for them would judge arithmetic that never runs, and `wheel_intent_at` is a READ and records nothing, because a census that moved the record while answering 'what would a wheel here do' is R1736's own lesson built into the framework. `scene/pointer_arrival` publishes it for EVERY surface in one spelling, with the population taken from the SCENE and not from the arrival store -- a report built by walking what the store holds could only list surfaces a pointer already reached, so 'nothing drifted' would be satisfied by a run that pointed at nothing; `never` is a row, and that row carries no counts and no position. THE GATE THIS ROUND WROTE WAS DEFECTIVE IN THE WAY R1736 NAMED, and its own re-measurement is what caught it: the first draft kept only the last arrival, so `RealPointer.__exit__` claimed to check every arrival a session caused while actually checking ONE -- the same shape as `scene/pointer_target` probing nine points where only the middle could convict. The framework counts now (`SurfaceArrivals`), the evidence kept is the FIRST drift rather than the last, and the report carries `delivered` and `drifts` so a caller can tell a clean run from an empty one. AND THE COST OF MEASURING KILLED WHAT IT MEASURED: querying after every move is a round trip plus a process per pixel, which loaded this host enough to time out the BOOT of the next screen the sweep was about to reach (exit 2). With the tally the query is once per screen, and 6,015 arrivals across five screens run in 110 seconds. THE FLOOR IS ABOVE US ON ONE AXIS AND THIS PAYS IT, built and run at 6.11.1 rather than read: an outside observer there can ask ANY widget where the pointer is in that widget's own frame with the widget storing nothing, exact over 400 columns and 300 rows, no misses. What it cannot do is answer this question -- its answer is where the CURSOR IS, not where the event ARRIVED: a press delivered to a child at (37,21) followed by moving the cursor leaves it answering (300,250), and across the five types such a record could live on there are 245 declared properties and 195 declared methods, of which 3 are point-typed (all the widget's own position in its parent) and 0 methods return a point. None is a delivered position, a synthesised event's position is unreadable, and it never compares its own two accounts. FOUR SCREENS WERE MISSING R1714's OWN LINE: `into_layout` exists so a caller applies it without first asking whether a screen pans, and four of the five self-hit-testing screens did not, each therefore having a hit test right at one offset and wrong at every other. VERIFIED: core 3,835 + rpc 1,289 + runtime 585; a new demo whose C section walks 600 columns and 600 rows on each of the five screens with the machine's own pointer -- 6,015 arrivals counted by the framework, 0 drifted -- with `strayed` measured live through a real capture lock on a grid painted at (20,110), which proves the origin subtraction at the same time; the seven pre-existing real-pointer demos re-run green under the new teardown gate. The debt that opened this closed with all three of its unmeasured items measured: the round trip, that a pointer selection speaks, and that the selection is VISIBLE (the list's own highlight moves to the pressed row and the derived pane redraws).

an application counts the sections it was judged on, and the count is part of the verdict. Declared `none` on the R1737 precedent, which is the same shape: this round builds an instrument and pays a measurement debt with it, and a new introspection READ is not what the api axis is judged on -- that axis is stabilisation (schemas, versioning, deprecation), none of which moved. No widget, no gesture, no axis re-judged against measured evidence. WHAT THE ROUND FOUND AT ITS START, over the running application's own wire rather than by reading it: standing in each of the tool's six open sections in turn, the application's `conformance` slot answered `specified 8, reproduced 8` from every one of them; two sections published a verdict about their own surfaces IF you already knew their tag; four published nothing at all. The headline is TRUE ABOUT THE RAIL -- eight navigation seats, eight reproduced -- and read as a statement about the tool, which is how it reads, it was wrong. The four silent sections were not failing a check, they were ABSENT FROM THE POPULATION, and no slot, test or report anywhere named them. That is R1737's lesson one level up (a gate existing and a gate's coverage being deliberate are different claims) and the repair is the same: make the framework count, make the population derived. THE FRAMEWORK HALF: `pinion_core::conformance` gains a TYPED report (`SurfaceStanding`, `DocumentReport`, `SpecDocument::report`) because the wire form was the only form and a wire form is where a count goes to stop being a count -- several specified sections could each be serialised and no two of them could be added together; `wire` now DERIVES from `report`, asserted equal, so the count an application publishes and the count it computes cannot disagree about one build. `WidgetView::conformance` (default `None`) and `Screen::conformance` (NO default): the asymmetry is the decision, since a hook required of every binding in this tree would be edits that say nothing, while a screen written directly against `Screen` is a host's own inline page -- the one place where 'is this section judged' is a live question somebody should answer out loud. `Mount<V>` forwards it, so a section publishes the same verdict in its own window and as a page. `ScreenRoster::conformance` walks THE ROSTER, one row per destination, so a section is missing from the report only by not being in the application; four arms and no catch-all, because `Judged`, `Unspecified`, `Inline` (the host paints this page itself, so this roster has no screen to ask) and `Closed` (carrying the destination's OWN reason) need four different pieces of work to change. It is deliberately not journey-keyed, unlike every accessor that hands out a screen, and the reason is written where the rule lives: a verdict about what a section is specified to contain is not behaviour, and an application that could only report on the section somebody happens to be standing in would be the defect being repaired. THE RULE THE TYPE EXISTS FOR: `conforms()` is FALSE while any open section is unjudged. An application assembled from sections must not be able to report conformance on the strength of the ones somebody happened to write a specification for. TWO THINGS THE INTEGRATION TEST FOUND RATHER THAN READING: a section's own wire is reachable only while the journey is standing in it -- this crate's central rule working -- so a client CANNOT assemble this verdict by asking the sections; it would have to navigate the tool to find out what the tool is, changing what the reader is looking at in order to measure it, and the host answering for all of them from anywhere is what makes the verdict possible at all. And every part of both judged sections' specifications is painted INSIDE THE HOST as well as in the section's own window, with `shell.appbar` / `shell.rail` / the seat's own rail entry surviving: 36 specified parts compared against the paint, the population taken from the report so the check cannot look at fewer sections than the application has. THE FLOOR, BUILT AND RUN AT 6.11.1 rather than remembered: a paged application of three pages, one page a part short of what it declares and one with the specified parts in the wrong order. Across the page-stack container, the tabbed container and a plain page, 312 members were scanned and ZERO name a specification, an expectation or a divergence -- there is nothing to write the statement in. The only channel a page has for declaring what it should contain is a compile-time per-class annotation, so three pages that built DIFFERENT things report the SAME specification. And the row that decides it: with the short page and the reordered page in it the container still answers `count() = 3`, has no member returning a verdict, a divergence or a count of pages judged, and nothing failed and nothing was reported. THE REMAINDER IS A TRACKED ARTIFACT: `docs/analyzer-sections-spec.json`, and unlike its siblings it is a claim about THIS BUILD rather than about the behaviour reference, so it does not repeat the seat list (the population is the rail pin's canon) and holds only what is owed -- four unjudged sections with the reason accepted for each, plus this round's own two. The gate asserts it EQUAL to the application's unjudged rows, so a section that starts answering must have its entry DELETED. The four are not one kind: two are the host's inline pages, one has no specification at all, and one HAS a specification it checks itself against inside a unit test of its own binary where the assembled application cannot see it -- and the framework cannot tell the last two apart, because only a screen knows and the hook has room for a report and none for a reason. VERIFIED: 10 counterfactuals, 10 caught -- six against the framework gate and four against the demo itself, two of which were rewritten after coming back BROKEN in the documented 'deleting a helper's only call site' class, which also measured that each judged section's part builder now has exactly one caller. pinion-core 3,839 plus pinion-screen and pinion-shell green; a new demo with 23 named checks; and the 30 demos that drive the shell or the two changed sections re-run.

Declared `none`: an engine pin bump plus one framework fact, no widget, no gesture and no axis re-judged. THE PIN moves 44 commits, a80b06d -> 7db6aeb, as the triple this repository already enforces -- the `vendor/sce` gitlink, both manifest `rev =` entries and the lock -- and `tools/pin_sync.py --check-dual-pin` caught the drift while only two of the three had moved, then reported `dual pin: SCE@7db6aeb (manifest = lock = vendor/sce)`. Every Tier-1 widget here is a generated statechart driven through ONE facade whose `send` returned `()`, so `the machine answered me` and `the machine threw it away` were the same value -- and they are not recoverable by looking, because a self transition, a targetless internal transition and a discard all leave the configuration alone. `pinion_core::widgets::Sent` is the first value in this framework that separates them, derived from the engine's discard counter across one drive rather than from a second account of the same fact; `Widget::send` and `App::send` both answer it, and no call site had to change because it is deliberately not `#[must_use]` -- 507 sites drive a statechart here and nearly all are a widget acting on its own gesture, so forcing five hundred `let _ =` would teach a reader to ignore the one thing worth reading. THE REMAINDER, MEASURED RATHER THAN ESTIMATED: the wire still cannot say it, because a widget's `send` invoke path answers with the resulting state name and for a discarded event that is the same name a self transition would give, so an agent gets a success meaning nothing happened; 21 demos drive that path, which makes refusing there a round with its own population. VERIFIED: workspace check and clippy clean on the new revision, fmt, pinion-core 3,841 + rpc 1,289 + widget-paint 900 + runtime 734 + shell across 29 test targets with 0 failed, and 42 demos that drive a statechart symbolically re-run green against release binaries built on the bump.

the wire says when an event went nowhere, and the round's own measurement decided how. Declared `none`: a refusal on an existing action surface, no widget and no axis re-judged. THE POPULATION WAS RE-MEASURED FIRST AND THE NUMBER WAS WRONG -- R1739 recorded 21 demos on the `send` path, having counted only the literal `invoke("…/send"` call form; counting every demo that names a `/send` path gives 38, and the corrected number is what the round was judged against. THE DESIGN WAS THEN DECIDED BY RUNNING IT, three passes: refusing is this tree's idiom (a refusal reaches the person) and reporting beside the state is the safe one, and which is right depends on how many demos legitimately send an event that goes nowhere -- which nobody knew. Button only, all 38: ZERO failures. Plus checkbox and toggle, all 38 again: ONE. With that one's clause split, all 38 again: zero. THAT ONE IS THE ROUND'S REAL RESULT AND IT IS A FINDING, NOT A BREAKAGE: `r1639_a_widget_publishes_its_verbs` drives every name a widget publishes and its clause said in as many words that a refusal is the failure and any answer is a pass, because it tests the VOCABULARY and not the sequencing. Under this round a published name can fail a second way, and the demo could not tell the two apart; it can now, but only by reading the PROSE -- `InvokeError` has exactly one refusal variant and `RefusalReason` is a bare sentence, so "this widget has no such event" and "this configuration does not answer it", which need different fixes, arrive as the same kind. Giving the discard its own kind reaches the RPC error mapping, `WIRE_TYPES` and every consumer matching on the enum, so it is recorded as owed rather than started. THE MECHANISM: `widget_core::require_landed` is the one place the tree decides what a discard means on the wire, beside `require_event` which answers the other question a symbolic drive asks, and its sentence names the state that did not answer -- "nothing answered it" without saying where leaves a client re-deriving the one fact that would explain it. `Widget::discarded` exposes the monotone counter because an `*External`'s own `send` runs the intent pipeline in between and cannot reach `Sent`; reading it either side of a drive is the shape the engine's documentation recommends, so it is not a second account. Three of thirty send-bearing surfaces refuse today and the remainder is a census with a shape rather than a grind list: 21 expose their inner widget and take the same two lines, 9 hold their statechart differently and are where the design question is. VERIFIED: pinion-core 3,843 including two new wire tests on the button -- one asserting a published event out of a configuration that does not answer it is refused NAMING THAT STATE and that the same event lands one state along, so the refusal is about the configuration and not the name; and one asserting a TARGETLESS transition is not a refusal, which is the mistake a check derived from comparing states would make -- plus fmt, workspace clippy, and the 38-demo population green.

the engine pin moves again, one commit, and the honest report is that there is nothing new to consume. Declared `none`: a pin bump with no source change. 7db6aeb -> e0fdd46 is a single upstream commit, test-only (it gives the invoke half the guards the send half already had), so it adds no API and this round does not manufacture a consumption to look larger -- R1739 consumed what the previous 44 commits brought and this one had nothing to bring. WHAT IT DID FIND IS A SEQUENCING RULE, FOUND BY TRIPPING OVER IT: the bump was begun while the previous round's push was still in flight, and the push was REFUSED with `pre-push: pinion's SCE pin disagrees with itself`, because the dual-pin gate reads the WORKING TREE AND INDEX and not the commit being pushed. The commit was fine; the tree around it was mid-bump. The gate was right and the ordering was wrong -- a pin bump is not a background task to start while something else is being published. AND THE FAILURE ARRIVED WEARING THE WRONG FACE: the harness reported the push as completed, exit code 0, while the recorded status was 1 and `git ls-remote` still showed the previous round's commit. This workspace already has that rule written down -- judge a push by the status stamped into a file and by the remote ref, never by the wrapper -- and this is the run that would have published a false claim of success without it. VERIFIED: `pin_sync.py --check-dual-pin` reports `dual pin: SCE@e0fdd46 (manifest = lock = vendor/sce)`, and pinion-core 3,843 library tests green -- unchanged from the count on the revision before it, which is the expected result for a test-only upstream commit and is stated because an unchanged number is evidence too.

a screen judges the surfaces that are on screen and says which are not, so the node lab publishes its inspector verdict inside the assembled tool. Declared `none`: a framework fact plus a section made answerable, no widget, no gesture and no axis re-judged against measured evidence. WHAT WAS MEASURED FIRST, because the review that asked for this could have been answered wrongly in either direction. The facilities take a worktree better than expected: `core.hooksPath=.githooks` is a RELATIVE path and git resolves it against the worktree root, so each worktree runs its own hooks with no `extensions.worktreeConfig` needed (`rev-parse --git-path hooks` answers `.githooks` at the root and `../../.githooks` two levels down); `bx` already knows about worktrees at line 1896 and derives its remote directory from `basename $(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)`, so two worktrees get different remote directories AND different locks; and the machine-wide sweep timer finds a new one for free, because it discovers projects with `find $HOME -maxdepth 3 -type l -name target` and `$HOME/pinion-wt/<name>/target` is exactly depth 3. BUT THE LEDGER IS A HARD SERIALISATION POINT AND THAT IS THE WHOLE FINDING: `docs/.atomic/workspace.atomic.json` is one file of 14 MB and 120,741 lines, and resolving a merge conflict in it IS the hand edit CLAUDE.md forbids, so a parallel round-closure has no correct resolution -- only "drop one side and re-apply through the CLI". `.gitattributes` now says so in git's own vocabulary: `-merge` on the store, because a SUCCESSFUL auto-merge is worse than a failed one (it produces a store nobody authored), and `merge=union` on `docs/phase-b-rounds.tsv`, which is the only append-only file here -- deliberately not the other `docs/*.tsv` budgets, since those are rewritten wholesale by their tool's `--write-budget` and a union merge there would resurrect stale rows and inflate a ratchet silently. THE TOOL: `tools/worktree.sh` creates DETACHED worktrees, so no branch exists and the ratified single-linear-main history is untouched. It exists because four things about this machine do not follow a bare `git worktree add` and all four fail QUIETLY -- the `target/` symlink onto the fixed-size compressed volume (without it cargo materialises a real `target/` on the root filesystem, uncompressed and unswept, which is the 2026-07-29 full-disk precondition rebuilt), submodule population, the shared headless display number (two worktrees sweeping at once draw into each other's screen and both readings are garbage), and teardown. THREE DEFECTS WERE FOUND BY RUNNING IT AND THE SELFTEST HAD PASSED ON ALL THREE. (1) `git worktree remove` REFUSES a worktree containing submodules, and this repo always has two -- so the obvious teardown does not work at all; worse, the obvious fix is destructive, because `submodule deinit` rewrites `submodule.<name>.url` in `.git/config` and worktrees SHARE that config, so tearing down an exploration worktree would strip the MAIN tree's submodule configuration. Removal now goes the way git documents for a worktree whose directory is gone -- delete it, then `prune` -- and the main tree's `submodule status` was checked afterwards. (2) `--init --recursive` was over-reach: the main tree deliberately leaves `vendor/sce`'s four nested submodules un-populated, so recursion cloned four repositories over the network that the main tree does not have. A worktree must MIRROR the main tree, not maximise it. (3) THE WORST ONE, AND IT IS THIS PROJECT'S OWN RECURRING SHAPE: the submodule verification was `submodule status --recursive | grep -q '^-'`, and on a run where git exited FATAL there were no `-` lines, so the check printed "verified: every submodule is populated". It also never said how many submodules it had looked at, so a status listing nothing would have passed too. Both halves are the same defect -- a check must distinguish its outcomes and must state its population -- and the repair is `classify_submodule_status(rc, output)` as a pure function with four verdicts (`failed`/`empty`/`unpopulated`/`ok`), each one a regression test for a bug that actually shipped in that file. AND THE PROHIBITION IS NOW ENFORCED RATHER THAN PRINTED: `add` used to merely print that a worktree may not commit, push or touch the ledger, and printing is not a gate -- this project already paid for that difference when a stop-the-line rule lived only in a gitignored prose file until R1495. `.githooks/lib/worktree-guard.sh` refuses both operations from a linked worktree, discriminating on the measured fact that `--absolute-git-dir` equals `--git-common-dir` in the main tree and is `<common>/worktrees/<name>` in a linked one -- a test that reads no path convention, so it holds for a worktree made by hand anywhere. It sits ahead of `mnemosyne_resolve` in pre-commit (a commit refused for standing in the wrong tree should not first pay a minute of tool build) and AFTER the library tests in pre-push (that hook's stated rule is that it does not decide with libraries it has not verified, and this is one). `PINION_WRITE_FROM_WORKTREE=1` overrides it loudly, and exists precisely because `--no-verify` already exists and disables EVERY gate: a named override records which rule was set aside. VERIFIED: hook libraries 129 assertions (was 120; the nine new ones drive all three verdicts plus the cases a lazier comparison would fail -- a trailing slash, a path that merely starts with the common dir, an empty override string); `worktree.sh --selftest` 30 checks, now run by pre-push so the tool cannot rot; and the gate was RUN, not reasoned about -- a real worktree created, a `git commit --allow-empty` there refused with rc=1 recorded to a file and the worktree's HEAD unmoved, the override releasing it, the main tree unaffected, and the worktree torn down with the main tree's submodules and the build-cache volume checked clean afterwards. The block matched `[Rr]ound[- ](\d+)`, and this store holds THREE key forms that interleave rather than succeed one another -- `Round 1708.4`, `R1742`, a bare `408` -- with the R-form the majority and what every recent round uses. So it read the newest entry as `Round 1708.4` when the real one was R1742, and framed a 34-round outage that did not exist. Measured with a reader that knows all three: the ledger is continuous from R1360 to R1742, the true gap is R1743-R1745, and a separate historic outage nobody had noticed sits at R1266-R1359 (86 of the 101 rounds in all of history that have no entry). The owner decision the debt asked for -- is the instruction canon or is the practice -- was therefore unnecessary: 383 consecutive rounds had kept the instruction. THE ROOT CAUSE IS ONE LAYER DOWN AND IT IS WHY R1744 WAS NOT CARELESS: there was no way to ASK. Both available readers answer wrongly. The hand regex above is one; the other is the documented tool, `mnemosyne-cli query --list-changelog`, which promises "round order, oldest first" and `--limit N` as "the newest N" and in fact groups by key FORM and sorts lexicographically inside each group, so its newest fourteen end `R999, SCE-RFC-002-004, round-14, round-15` -- it answers Round 15 for the latest entry, off by 1,730. Its `--changelog-entry` also requires the historical form (`R1742` resolves, `R1519` is rejected because that round's key is `Round 1519`), so the same question needs different syntax per round. A rule nobody can query is a rule nobody can keep. That is upstream in `vendor/mnemosyne` and NOT fixable from a pinion session, so it is registered as a debt with the fix described (derive the sort key from the parsed number; classify keys that name no round instead of burying them last). THE MECHANISM: `tools/changelog_rounds.py` is this repo's canonical reader and its gate. It parses the round number and requires only that any sub-round label EXIST -- the shapes in the store are `.4`, `.2a`, `b`, `.109.0`, `.D.1`, `.1.b.1.tui`, `.A`, and enumerating them was never going to hold -- and a key whose form it cannot read is a REFUSAL rather than a skip, because a skipped key is a round it would silently miscount. The floor is not shared and is deliberately older (R1359 vs the tally's R1519), because the ledger's claim is older than the tally. THE THREE MISSING ENTRIES WERE BACKFILLED, not grandfathered: reconstructed from each round's commit, its row in this file (6,758 + 5,113 + 3,472 chars, written by the rounds themselves) and its memory topic file, with the first paragraph of each entry saying it is a reconstruction and its verification bullets restricted to what those sources record. THE ROUND'S FIRST DELIVERABLE IS A TEST, NOT THE OPTIMISATION, and the reason is the sharpest thing here: the consumer had the RIGHT numbers and drew a wrong conclusion from them -- it read the path count as glyph outlines being re-encoded per frame and asked first for a glyph atlas -- because nothing in this repository said what a grid's draws are OF. Measured with a fixture over 8x4 and 16x4 at ink 0, 3 and 8: paths track the CELLS and are untouched by the ink, so a glyph is not encoded as an outline path in this pipeline; and draws equals paths plus glyph_runs exactly, so a grid has no third source of draws. My own reasoning was wrong TWICE before that fixture ran -- first inferring the attribution from a segments-per-path ratio alone, then reading the excess over the cell count as the ink when it is a constant, which a fixture whose ink count and constant were BOTH 3 cannot tell apart. The tests are differential for exactly that reason: the law is the DIFFERENCE between two grids, never an absolute that pins the frame's constant. THE GROUND SKIP IS THE ITEM THE CONSUMER'S REPORT DOES NOT CONTAIN and it is the larger half. Pass 0 already fills the whole node rect in the palette's default background before any cell, so a default-background cell was painting that colour over itself, and a terminal screen is overwhelmingly default background. This was not knowable when the debt was written: that file says the node cannot know what is behind it, and in fact the node lays its own ground. Guarded on opacity, because painting a translucent colour over itself composites twice and is a different pixel. The extraction into `paint_cell_backgrounds` is not tidying: the painter had reached 103 lines against a 100-line lint and its own doc comment already called the work two grid-wide passes, so decomposition was the fix and an allow attribute would have been the workaround. VERIFIED: fmt clean, pinion-runtime 738 passed, pinion-shell green, clippy -D pedantic clean over both crates, counterfactuals 2/2 CAUGHT written as wrong answers rather than absent ones, and -- because this is a PAINT change -- the 12 TextGrid PIXEL tests run locally with `--ignored` rather than deferred to CI, two of them exactly the cases this could have broken (a trailer's inherited background inside a merged run, and the gutter fill the skip relies on). So the pixel-identity claim is a result and not an argument. STATED LIMIT, not papered over: the opacity guard cannot be falsified by a test, because `Palette` exposes no mutator and a translucent default background cannot be constructed from outside the crate. SELF-GREP FIRED: the same GridBuffer is now folded into runs in TWO places with two different notions of "the same" -- the snapshot's six-tuple RunKey and this pass's single resolved background -- registered as its own debt rather than lifted, because they are two opinionated copies and not three mechanical ones; pass 2's glyph batching will be the third fold, so the next round reads that file first. one grid is folded into runs by ONE rule, and the second paint pass folds its glyphs and its rules TOGETHER so that batching them changes no pixel. Declared `perf` because it removes the remaining per-cell draw the consumer's 4 fps frame was made of -- 3,400 `draw_glyphs` calls become one per ink run, and a run's underline and strikethrough become one span each instead of one per cell. WHAT FORCED IT was R1748's own mandatory self-grep: the same GridBuffer was already being folded into runs elsewhere, by a different idea of "the same" -- the scene/snapshot readback's six-tuple against the painter's single resolved background. Both right for their purpose, nothing relating them, so the run boundaries an agent reads off the wire and the rectangles actually painted could differ with no statement anywhere that they may. It was registered as a debt with the deferral this project's rule allows for two OPINIONATED copies; THE OWNER WITHDREW THE DEFERRAL ("do not defer even mechanical duplication"), so it is paid in the round after the one that found it. THE LIFT MEASURED SOMETHING THE DEBT DID NOT KNOW: the SGR-7 reverse swap was duplicated too, and the second copy was a HALF -- the terminal backend computed only an effective background, inline. Its old doc argued the swap belonged to the renderer because a snapshot leaves it to "a renderer"; true about the snapshot and never true about the NUMBER of renderers, so an attribute that also swapped would have been honoured by one and silently ignored by the other. THE CONSISTENCY CONDITION IS NOW A TEST, which is what the debt asked for: a narrow key's run boundaries are a subset of the wide key's, because every part of a narrow key is a function of the wide one's components. Its sibling asserts the three keys fold one row DIFFERENTLY first, because two keys accidentally equal would satisfy the refinement trivially -- the vacuous-fixture failure this project keeps meeting. And a counterfactual aims one level below both: a background key that reads the FOREGROUND term still refines the style key and still folds, and paints the wrong colour, so REFINEMENT IS NOT CORRECTNESS. THE DRAW-ORDER PROBLEM WAS SOLVED RATHER THAN AVOIDED: batching glyphs alone reorders a frame, because a cell's underline is stroked between its own glyph and the next cell's, so a pooled run lands wholly under or over rules it used to interleave with and a glyph that overflows its cell is a different pixel. Folding glyphs and rules on one key keeps the per-cell order at run granularity -- and a run's rule as one span is what this painter already wanted in words. THE POOL REFUSES TO SHAPE MORE THAN ONE CLUSTER: handing the shaper a run's text would let kerning and ligatures move glyphs across cell boundaries, wrong in a monospaced grid, so shaping stays per-cluster and cached and only the EMISSION is pooled; the pool also breaks on the face and size it was shaped for and flushes before a synthesised block or box glyph, whose geometry is a fill that used to precede the next cell's glyph. VERIFIED: fmt, core+runtime, rpc+tui+shell, clippy -D pedantic over five crates, all judged by an rc written to a FILE; counterfactuals 4/4 CAUGHT as wrong answers; and the 12 TextGrid PIXEL tests run locally with --ignored TWICE, once for the rewritten pass and once after the counterfactual driver restored the sources, because they are the only check a draw-order change has. Self-grep re-run finds NO hand-rolled row fold left; the terminal backend still writes cell by cell, which is not a third fold because a terminal buffer is per-cell by the medium. ONE TEST WAS WRONG TWICE BEFORE IT WAS RIGHT and both drafts are recorded in its doc: the first READ THE HOST (it asserted a Latin letter beside a Hangul syllable needs two faces, and the resolved monospace face covers both here, so the pool would have been one either way -- it failed loudly only because it asserted its own premise), the second INVENTED FACES (synthetic blobs are not font files and vello parses what it is handed, so the flush panicked). STATED LIMIT carried unchanged from R1748: the opacity guard on the ground-skip cannot be falsified, Palette exposes no mutator. NOT DONE HERE: the profile's 44% in font-table parsing, which is the debt's third item and its own round.

THIS ROUND CORRECTS THE ONE BEFORE IT, and the correction is the more useful half. Declared `none`: a correction plus an engine-guarantee test, no widget, no gesture, no axis re-judged. R1750 recorded that the engine revision it adopted had NOT brought its macrostep bound to the Rust backend, and shipped a handoff asking upstream to add one. THAT IS FALSE: the bound arrived in that very commit -- `backends/rust/runtime/src/engine.rs` gained 194 lines including `pub(crate) const MAX_MACROSTEP_MICROSTEPS: usize = 1000` beside a 253-line fixture. The ledger cannot be amended, so the correction is filed as its own entry, which is the mechanism this project already uses for a superseded judgment. WHY THE MEASUREMENT WAS WRONG is what makes it worth a round: R1750 grepped `tools/codegen/templates/rust/`, found nothing that bounds a macrostep, and concluded the bound was absent from Rust. What it had actually found is that RUST IS NOT C11 -- Rust keeps the macrostep loop in the runtime crate and so does Go (engine.go holds the same 1000); the only backend carrying the bound in a TEMPLATE is C11, because C11 inlines everything into generated source, which is also why that one file was the only place with fourteen keyword hits. The signal was real and the reading of it was not. AND R1750 WAS CAREFUL IN THE OTHER DIRECTION, which is why this is a lesson and not carelessness: it found two Rust hits that LOOK like a bound -- a lint "suppression budget" and a MAX_MICROSTEP_DEDUP_SLOTS slot count -- and excluded both correctly. It guarded against false positives and then searched the one place the thing could not be. AN ABSENCE MUST BE MEASURED MORE WIDELY THAN A PRESENCE: a presence is proven wherever you find it, an absence is only true once every place it could live has been counted, and "generated code is where this feature lives" was an unexamined premise rather than a measurement. THE EXPOSURE R1750 CLAIMED DOES NOT EXIST, now measured rather than argued: the generated machines only implement StatePolicy, the loop belongs to Engine

, and widgets/widget.rs plus app.rs both drive it through engine.process_event, so twelve widget statecharts and the window topology all run inside the budget. WHAT THE ERROR LEFT BEHIND IS REAL WORK and this round does it: nothing here asserted that the budget protects OUR machines -- upstream's fixture proves the engine, a different claim from proving the path a widget takes. R1750 said such a test could not be written because it would not terminate; that followed from the false premise, and with the bound present it terminates by construction. So `fixtures/self_answering_raise.scxml` is a chart whose transition answers its own with another, and three assertions cover it: the engine stops the macrostep and COUNTS it, the machine still takes an event from outside the chain afterwards, and a second entry spends the budget a second time. Their failure mode is unusual and is why they are worth having -- if the bound were absent they would not FAIL, they would not RETURN, so reaching an assertion at all is half the proof; and what they assert is an ACCOUNT, never a duration, because "it finished within N seconds" is the shape that goes flaky on a slow runner. VERIFIED: pinion-core + pinion-runtime green, clippy clean, fmt clean, each judged by an rc written to a file. COUNTERFACTUALS 3/3 CAUGHT, but only after a first attempt scored 1/3 and BOTH failures were mine in the two shapes the driver documents -- one did not compile because it replaced a call with a binding that used nothing, which is an ABSENCE where the rule demands a WRONG ANSWER (re-aimed at e.stop(), a machine stopped instead of entered); the other PASSED because it clamped an assertion rather than breaking a mechanism, and a clamp is not a defect anything arrives at, whereas reading the WRONG COUNTER is exactly what a consumer does when an engine exposes several (re-aimed at unattended_scheduler_steps(), caught at once). a frame record says WHICH FUNCTION its render number measured, and a window says how many of each kind it averaged over. Declared `perf` because it retires a pro-tool-performance item on measurement and makes the frame accounting readable. WHAT FORCED IT: the grid debt's third item asks for a font-table handle cache on a consumer's 44.4% profile, and that same file says in its own words to do items 1 and 2 first and then MEASURE AGAIN. R1748 and R1749 did them, so this round measured -- and THE ITEM'S PREMISE IS FALSE ON THIS TREE, so it is corrected rather than implemented. One app, 80x24, sixty frames each way: ticked, mean render 8,452us against encode 102 and build 50; screenshotted, 10,344us against encode 104 and build 54. Shaping plus vello encode, which is where a font-table lookup lives, is 152us = 1.8% of the frame in BOTH regimes, while render_us is 97.8% with acquire_us at 5us so it is not a vsync wait either. The consumer's 44.4% was true of THEIR app at ten times the cells on a different font stack. THE ANSWER CAME FROM THE APP'S OWN FRAME ACCOUNTING, NOT FROM A PROFILE, and three profiles were taken first, each invalid for a DIFFERENT reason: the first sampled the app IDLE (82.58% in one kernel address -- a blinking cursor repaints once or twice a second); the second forced 128 frames over scene/screenshot and sampled ITS OWN PROBE (_copy_from_iter 64.5% plus serde 21%, actual render 0.81%, because that RPC ships pixels as JSON); the third profiled the pixel tests, which have no RPC channel, and sampled wgpu's SHADER COMPILATION because twelve short tests have no steady state. "A profile came out" and "that profile is about this question" are different claims and the second must be argued every time. WHAT READING render_us THROUGH THOSE THREE EXPOSED: the submit is an EITHER/OR -- a frame runs capture_rgba8 or render, never both -- so one field reported two functions under one name, measured 22% apart, with nothing saying which; and the reading most likely to be taken was the least interpretable, because an agent asks for screenshots, so an agent's frame timings were capture frames. THE DEMO THEN FOUND A SECOND LAYER OF THE SAME DEFECT: asserting on `last` FAILED, because `last` is the most recent frame RECORDED and an idle paint lands between a request and the read, so a client cannot use it to prove anything about its own request -- hence a per-window count, which is also what makes mean_render_us readable at all since a mean over a mixed window is a mean over two functions. VERIFIED: three crates green, clippy clean, fmt clean, each judged by an rc written to a FILE; blast radius taken as WHO READS A FRAME TIMING rather than what was edited, so all 18 demos that read scene/frame_timings ran, zero failures; the new demo drives both regimes on one window and reads the flag back over RPC (ticked captured_frames=0, shot captured_frames=11). COUNTERFACTUALS 3/3 CAUGHT after a first run scored 2/3, and the PASSED one was the finding: NOTHING IN cargo test ASSERTED captured_frames -- only the demo watched it, and a demo is not in the gate a counterfactual runs, so an inverted count would have shipped. Two tests now pin it with the capturing frame deliberately in the MIDDLE of the window, because a fold taking either end would still be right about a one-element window and wrong there, and an inverted fold answers 2. The wire test gives its two frames the SAME duration on purpose, since a fixture where the capturing frame were also the slower one would pass while testing nothing. SELF-GREP: this is the FOURTH instance in one file of a number carrying a qualifier that says what it is of (settle_passes with settled, gpu_us with gpu_timing_supported, and these two) -- a recurring SHAPE rather than duplicated code, so what was lifted is the NAME, into the module doc, so a later round applies it deliberately instead of rediscovering it. CARRIED: render_us still holds a readback whole rather than splitting it, which needs the backend to time its own internals exactly as acquire_us needed in R1361.1; and WHAT THE 97.8% IS remains unexplained, now the grid debt's live question in place of the font-table item this round retired -- it is CPU time recording and submitting, with the vsync block already split out at 5us and the GPU's own clock at 543us, so it is neither waiting nor the GPU.

a list drags. `ScrollNode::with_content_drag(ContentDrag::Grab)` makes a primary-button press that strays past the framework's click-vs-drag threshold pan the region it started in, and the row it landed on keeps the tap. Declared `catalog` and not `modelview`: that axis is a DATA path -- selection models, section headers, column axes -- while this is an interaction vocabulary a shared container publishes, the family `gesture` / `pinch-zoom` / `raw-pointer` are filed under and the same family as this axis's standing wheel-reach item. FORCED BY A CONSUMER, at 430x932: eighteen rows, nine on screen, every row a tap target, and a press-and-drag moved the offset by 0 px while opening the pressed row. THE REPORT'S DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG IN THE DIRECTION THAT MATTERS and correcting it is most of the round's value. It grepped `widgets/scroll.rs`, found no `pan` / `drag` / `pointer` / `fling`, and concluded the machinery was absent; the machinery is in `pinion-runtime/src/input.rs` and it included a LEFT-BUTTON pan already -- `left_pan_down` / `left_pan_up` / `left_pan_in_flight` (R882), with press-time pinned targets, the `DragLatch` dead zone, the sub-pixel remainder carry and the swallowed-press pairing. The real gap was one line in `core_shell.rs`: `if self.held_keys.space()`, so the primary pan was armed ONLY by a keyboard chord, which is the design tool's hand-tool dialect and not the dialect a finger speaks. AN ABSENCE MEASURED IN ONE FILE IS NOT AN ABSENCE, which is R1751's lesson arriving from a consumer this time. WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW IS AN ESCALATION, not a gesture. The chord dialect SWALLOWS the press -- no `PointerDown`, no focus -- because it is armed before the press and nothing else can want it; a list needs the opposite, so the press reaches the row, and only on the threshold crossing does the region take the pointer over, cancel the widget's press so it is not left latched, and drop the press record so the release resolves in the pan channel and `pointer_up` never runs at all. That is strictly stronger than the R794 trailing-click suppression it replaces here: no activation, no caret, no auto-repeat can survive the pan. `pan_down`'s own exclusivity guard REFUSED a pan while `press_gestures` held the pointer, and that guard was precisely what blocked the handover. A PRESS ON BARE CONTENT ARMS AT PRESS TIME instead, because there is no widget to be ambiguous with -- the gap doc asked for "a press that started inside the scroll container", and a press on the padding between rows reaches nothing, so the container may have it at once, exactly `pan_down`'s reasoning for the middle button. It opens in the DEAD ZONE, so a click on empty background is still a click that moved nothing. THE WALK CLIMBS. `Scene::content_drag_target_at` is NOT `scroll_target_at` plus a filter on the answer: a region that declines content drags is TRANSPARENT to the gesture, so an ancestor that takes them still gets the pan -- the W3C scroll chain -- and testing only the deepest node answers None for exactly the nested arrangement that strands a finger. Both walks share one descent, lifted rather than copied, so the region a pan pins and the region a wheel resolves cannot come to mean different things. DEFAULT IS `Off`, opposite to `AutoScroll`, and the asymmetry is the argument: auto-scroll EXTENDS a gesture the user is already making, a content drag CLAIMS one, so defaulting it on would silently convert every rubber band, cell sweep and marquee in the tree into a pan. THE HANDOVER IS AN EDGE, NOT A LEVEL: `track_press_drag` now reports the rising edge, because gating on the level would re-walk the paint tree on every move of every drag in the tree while the answer is a property of the press POINT, which does not move. The cancel count is what a test can see the difference on -- a level gate still produces a correct-looking offset. TWO OF THE DRIVER'S OWN BUGS ARE THE ROUND'S OTHER FINDING, both coordinate-space: a row's snapshot rect is CONTENT-LOCAL, so reading a row centre and clicking it as a window coordinate aimed two rows away after a 200 px scroll, and a `Scene::Scroll` publishes `viewport` rather than `rect` because it has two rectangles and naming either one `rect` makes the pair ambiguous. The demo now derives only the row CHOICE and hands the row to the harness BY PATH, so the conversion has one home, and asserts the opened row equals the row it chose -- a cross-check between the two, not a restatement. VERIFIED: workspace clippy green, fmt clean, pinion-core 3859 + pinion-runtime + pinion-shell + pinion-rpc + pinion-tui + the example all green, and `tools/demos/hello_content_drag.py` PASSes over the wire -- a drag on a row pans 0 -> 213 (the clamped maximum) with `opened` null and `cancels` 1, a tap opens the row it aimed at and scrolls nothing, and a drag on bare content pans 213 -> 93 with `cancels` unchanged. That third slot is load-bearing: without it the drag assertion passes on an app whose rows are simply dead. NOT DONE, named rather than implied: no inertia (a separate axis -- velocity estimate, deceleration curve, a frame tick to integrate on, and it changes where the content comes to rest), and focus stays where the press put it because the shell's press follow-ups ran before the escalation and are not rewound.

a frame timing says WHAT MADE IT. `scene/frame_timings` gains `adapter` -- name, device class, backend and a derived `hardware` verdict for the GPU stack every microsecond in the record was measured on. Declared `perf` because a pro-tool profiler that cannot state the premise of its own numbers is not a profiler, and this round proves that by exhibit: R1752 read `render_us`, found it was 97.8% of the frame, and wrote that into the ledger as a fact about pinion. IT WAS A FACT ABOUT THE DISPLAY THAT ROUND RAN ON, and that sentence is corrected in the R1754 entry because a frozen entry cannot be amended. THE ROUND'S OWN PLAN WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT, MID-ROUND, and that is the most valuable thing in it. The field was built on the assumption that a virtual framebuffer forces a software rasterizer, which would have made `device_class: cpu` the explanation. Asking the two displays instead of reasoning about them: same machine, same app, same scene at draws 133, `mean_render_us` was 10,384us on Xvfb :97 and 997,132us on the real Xorg :1 -- ninety-six-fold -- with the adapter answering IDENTICALLY both times (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Laptop GPU / vulkan / discrete / hardware true) and `gpu_us` 491us against 1,759us. A visible window on :1 measured 997,457us, so it is not a hidden-window artifact either. So the adapter is NECESSARY -- a bug report is not reproducible without it, and `cpu` is a real state on a host with no GPU -- and NOT SUFFICIENT, and every doc this round wrote says so, because a qualifier believed past its evidence is the exact failure the convention exists to prevent and this one had already been believed once. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT POINTED AT INSTEAD: 133 draws record and submit in microseconds and the GPU itself spent 1.8ms, so 997ms is neither, and the only other statement inside the timed span is `surface_texture.present()` -- a block on whoever consumes the swapchain, billed as work by a field documented as "record + submit, CPU-side" and "work only, acquire excluded". That is R1361.1's defect at the other end of the frame: that round split the ACQUIRE block out and left the PRESENT block in. Registered as its own debt and deliberately NOT built here, because it is a second larger change (trait method, forge template, phase partition, wire, census) and folding it in would make neither reviewable -- and the new demo asserts `present_us` is ABSENT, so the day it lands this round's stated limit fails loudly instead of going stale. THE FACT EXISTED AND NOTHING COULD READ IT: `GpuContext` held the adapter in a private field consumed only by its own `Debug` impl, reachable by a log line and by nothing else, while every duration pinion publishes is a measurement of it. THE VOCABULARY IS PINION'S: `GpuDeviceClass` / `GpuBackend` are closed enums beside the record following `PresentHealth` one line away, because a wire echoing wgpu's enums would change under AI clients that cannot be recompiled. THE SELF-GREP MOVED CODE: each token and verdict is spelled by the type that owns it (`as_str` / `is_hardware` / `draws`), this tree's idiom at 23 sites including the `Missed` / `Rung` pair the sibling `present_health_of` already reads -- the first draft had spelled them in the projector. VERIFIED: five crates green, workspace clippy and the doc gate green, counterfactuals 7/7 CAUGHT with fixtures built so no single-operand implementation passes (Cpu-on-Vulkan and Discrete-on-Noop disagree about WHICH term makes `hardware` false; three windows get IDENTICAL samples so only the qualifier can tell them apart), the wgpu mapping unit-tested rather than demo-only on R1752's lesson that demos are not in the counterfactual gate, and all 19 demos reading `scene/frame_timings` pass. NOT VERIFIED and stated: what the 997ms actually is -- the attribution to `present()` is by elimination, not isolation, and the debt note makes measuring it the first step of paying it.

The key-pattern header specifies three parts and reported the third, a box holding a text field, ABSENT while the frame plainly drew it. FLOOR, measured by building a probe against the reference toolkit 6.11.1 and running it: 768 members scanned across the page stack, the tabbed container, the table view, a plain page and two leaf widgets, and 0 name a verdict, a specification, evidence, a divergence or a canon; the structural answer for a page NEVER SHOWN is IDENTICAL to the page on screen, so a conformance check written there passes unchanged for a page nobody opened; 0 members mentioning paint return anything, and `grab()` renders a never-shown page on demand, so even the pixels do not distinguish it. An agent can drive a keystroke GESTURE over the wire and not just a keystroke: `scene/key` takes a burst, and the delivery it lands in is published as `scene/input_state`'s seventh axis. Declared `none`, and the near miss is the §7 `api` axis, considered and REJECTED for the same measured reason R1758 rejected it plus one of its own: that axis is judged on STABILISATION (method->type binding, version negotiation, deprecation, freeze, per-method error taxonomy), and this round ADDED wire surface that cannot be declared anywhere an agent can query -- `rpc/methods` publishes only name/occ/window, so "exactly one of key / keys", "an entry is a string or a {key,state} object" and "the target is required unless every stroke is a release" are discoverable only by being refused. Crediting `api` would credit a round for widening the undeclared surface, which moves that axis AWAY from its goal; the cost is recorded against the two-describing-surfaces debt instead, whose price has now moved from judgment prose to a live surface. THE HANDOFF WAS ALREADY ANSWERED: sprag's PINION-PR84 asked for an arrival timestamp on `pinion_core::event::KeyEvent` and R1658 had delivered the capability (`KeyArrival` = instant + batch, `KeyPress`, `WidgetCore::apply_key_press`) a hundred rounds earlier. Two of the report's four "gap proof" items are still true and two are now false, so a round reading only the true ones would have rebuilt what exists; and R1658's own finding re-measured as still true, that the named type has exactly ONE construction site in the tree, its own test, so building what was asked would have delivered nothing to anybody. The work was therefore R1658's residue, three open debts, and ALL THREE WERE LARGER THAN THEIR FILES SAID. FIRST, "an agent cannot send a burst" was HALF TRUE: `scene/type` already fans a string into one drain, so CHARACTER bursts had a door and what had none were the NAMED keys -- the arrows a repeat window is actually spent on, and exactly what the reported defect (a `-r` binding dragging a boundary ten cells, 3 of 6 failures under 2x CPU oversubscription, the lost presses reaching the user's shell as raw escapes) is made of. The `keys` array is alternative to `key` and rejected if both are given; entries are a bare name or `{key, state}`, and the per-entry edge is not decoration since a pan chord is `Space` down, the arrows, `Space` up, and the whole claim of that gesture is that the three arrived together. Parsing completes before anything is enqueued, so a malformed entry at index five leaves the inbox untouched -- a partial burst is worse than a rejected one, because the drain would deliver the surviving prefix as a COMPLETE delivery. SECOND, PUBLISHING THE READ AXIS EXPOSED AN INSTRUMENT THAT CONSUMED WHAT IT MEASURED. The question an agent has is a DISTANCE (did one request open one delivery, or three?) because both outcomes leave a different batch open than before, so equality separates nothing -- which is why `KeyBatch::ordinal` is published despite that type's own rule against arithmetic, with the rule still standing for Rust consumers who ask `arrived_with`. Then the measurement: EVERY RPC REQUEST RAN THE DRAIN AND THE DRAIN OPENED A DELIVERY UNCONDITIONALLY, so the two `scene/input_state` reads bracketing a burst each opened one and the difference read three. R1658 wrote "one drain is one delivery" and the drain implemented it literally; that was invisible while the arrival was a Rust-only fact and became a defect the moment the field was published. The rule is now "one drain THAT DISPATCHES A KEYSTROKE is one delivery", which is what it always meant, and the standing lesson is that an implementation harmless while unobservable must be re-read by the round that makes it observable. THIRD, THE TERMINAL'S RPC DRAIN HAD NO DELIVERY BOUNDARY AT ALL and no debt file knew: R1658 gave the terminal LOOP its boundary and left the drain without one, so a key injected over RPC into a TUI app inherited whichever delivery the last TYPED key had opened, claiming to have arrived alongside a keystroke it had nothing to do with, and a binding asking `arrived_with` would have honoured the pair -- §2 #6 asks the two backends not to disagree about the user's input and on this axis they did. FOURTH, the terminal boundary is tested as prescribed: `await_delivery` takes its `poll` as an argument, which was the whole of what stood in the way, and all three answers are asserted including that the availability question is asked FIRST, since it is about the moment the previous dispatch returned. VERIFIED: five crates green, workspace clippy green, `cargo doc --no-deps` green on those five, harness selftest 41 cases / 118 assertions, counterfactuals 7/7 CAUGHT -- and CF-2 also reddened R1658's OWN tests, which is the evidence this round's gate does not contradict R1658's contract. TWO EXISTING GATES CAUGHT THIS ROUND BEFORE ANY OF ITS OWN CHECKS DID (R1585.1's window-column probe, R1627's axis census), so re-running old gates found more than the new tests again. THE CLOSING AUDIT FOUND THREE FALSE CLAIMS IN THIS ROUND'S OWN COMMENTS, all written hours earlier and all fixed: that `#[non_exhaustive]` forced a wildcard (false in the DEFINING crate -- now an exhaustive match over all 27 variants, so the compiler is the gate rather than a grep); that the release check deferred to one predicate (it re-decided it three lines away as `== Up`); and that one object parser served both wire forms (it did not, and the duplicate is deleted). A RUSTC ICE WAS FOUND AND MIS-DIAGNOSED TWICE BEFORE THIS ENTRY CLOSED, and the isolation is recorded because the near miss was a false diagnosis entering a frozen ledger: `cargo doc -p hello-node-lab --no-deps` dies in rustc's rmeta encoder ("no resolutions for a doc link") at a PRIVATE `mod spec;`.
